blocks.h: A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
This book began with a single fact I could not put down.

The urge to breathe is not about running out of air. What makes a person desperate under water is waste gas building up, and the alarm that goes off is not measuring the thing that can kill them. The two timetables come apart. Which means the alarm fires long before there is real danger — and it also means the alarm can be finished, silent, satisfied, while the danger is still on its way.

And it can be trained out of you. That is the part I have not been able to leave alone. There is an entire sport built on teaching human beings to hear their own bodies screaming that they are dying and to file the screaming as noise. It works. It is taught kindly, by careful people, with tables and stopwatches and homework, and it produces divers who feel excellent in the last ten seconds before the lights go out.
The oldest alarm we have, the one that comes before language, the one no animal ignores. Trainable in a fortnight.

So the question the book is actually asking is: what else. What other alarms are measuring the wrong thing, and going off on timetables of their own, and what would happen to a person who was taught, patiently and correctly and by somebody who loved them, to stop listening.

Everything in these pages about what happens to a body at depth is drawn from the literature and is, as far as I have been able to establish, accurate. The colour dying in order. The heart down in the twenties with four seconds between beats. The chest squeezed smaller than empty and the smallest vessels giving way. The proteins that turn up in the blood afterwards, the same ones you would measure in a man who had been hit in the head. The sensed presence in the cold and the dark, which is so well documented in mountaineers and sailors and polar walkers that the coaching community has stopped remarking on it. The shaking on the surface, which ends roughly one competition dive in ten and which nobody finds remarkable. Feeling wonderful immediately beforehand.
I have invented nothing about the water. I have only removed the disbelief.

The other debt is to a coast on the other side of the world. For centuries the women of the Shima region of Japan dived on one breath, several times a day, for their entire working lives, and they had a word for what some of them met down there: tomokazuki, the companion diver. Not a stranger. Themselves, met at depth, identical in every particular except that one thing was slightly too long. It does not attack. It offers, and it waits, and you do not take what it offers. In 1939 the folklorist Iwata Junichi published a dozen of their accounts. The medical literature attributes the encounters to cold, exhaustion, isolation and running low, all at once, and is very likely correct, and I do not think the women of that coast would have found the correction interesting. They cared about what you did.
I am grateful to both bodies of work and I have tried to be honest with them.

One last thing, which is the only personal note in this. When I was a child a dervish came through the town where I was living — very tall, long-bearded, carrying everything he owned in a single bag. He was not in a hurry about anything, and I could not work out what he was doing, and it did not seem to me that a person could be that still on the outside and be still on the inside as well. It frightened me. I have thought about him for most of my life, and I thought about him constantly while writing this, because the thing I have put at the bottom of the Cut is exactly that stillness, and the whole question of the book is what has to be taken out of a person to produce it.
Chew Z
I. THE SPORT
ONE. 0 METRES
The woman comes up at eleven past nine and does everything right.

Sabine watches from the platform with her hands in her coat pockets. She is not required to watch. She is required to sign a form at the end of the day saying the water was managed, and the form does not ask whether she looked at it. But she has been coming out to the Cut for three weeks now and she has not yet found a way to stand on the platform without watching, so she watches.

The woman’s head breaks the surface and she does not gasp. That is the first thing. The untrained gasp — they come up and they haul at the air like it owes them, and the hauling is the most dangerous thing they will do all morning, because a body that has been running on nothing for two minutes will sometimes take that first great greedy pull and simply stop. The woman does not gasp. She lets her mouth open and takes a small breath, then a second, then a third, each one deeper than the last, building back up in steps the way you would walk up out of a cellar rather than jumping.

Then she reaches up and takes the mask off her face. She does not push it up onto her forehead. She takes it off, all the way, and holds it, because the rule is that the safety diver has to see your eyes and there is no argument about whether he can see them through glass.

She finds him. He is a metre away, treading, waiting, and has been waiting since the moment she left. She looks at him. She holds his eyes for a full three seconds, which is longer than it sounds when you are cold and your heart is somewhere down in the twenties and climbing.
She lifts her hand out of the water, and makes a circle of her thumb and forefinger, and holds it up.
“I’m okay,” she says.

The safety diver nods and says her time. Two minutes eleven. Thirty-one metres. She laughs, once, and the laugh goes out flat across the water and comes back off the slate walls a half-second later, and that is the only echo you get at the Cut. Everything else the walls keep.
Sabine takes her hands out of her pockets.

It is a ritual for proving that you are still yourself, and it is performed, always, by somebody whose judgement is the least reliable it will be all day. That is the thing about it that nobody says out loud. The first symptom of running low is not weakness. It is confidence. A diver forty seconds from the lights going out will tell you, sincerely, in a clear voice, with steady eyes, that she feels excellent. So the sport built a test she can fail without knowing, and made it mandatory, and made it short, and gave it to a man who is watching for the wobble in her jaw and the drift in her eyes and the half-beat of hesitation before the words.
Mask off. Eyes. Sign. I’m okay.
Four things. She got all four.
The Cut is a hole that men dug for money and then stopped digging.

Six generations of Ossay went down into it dry, with lamps, and cut slate out of the walls in blocks, and brought the blocks up, and roofed most of the north of the department with them. Then slate stopped being what anyone wanted and the company that owned the hole discovered it owed more than the hole was worth, and one morning in a year Sabine’s grandmother could remember, they turned off the pumps and went home.

A quarry is only ever dry on purpose. It took eleven years to fill. There was no ceremony about it. The water came up through the floor and in off the moor and down out of the sky and kept coming, and at some point in the middle of that decade the last of the machinery was hauled out and sold for the metal, and the men who had stripped it did a thorough job, because they were paid by weight. There is nothing down there now. That is a thing Sabine finds she has to tell people, and tell them twice, because they always want there to be something. A cage. A winch. A cart on a rail. They want the bottom of the water to be a museum.
It is silt and slate. Ninety-four metres of black and then a floor with nothing on it.

The town has no sea. The nearest coast is four hours in a car and it is a bad coast, all shingle and wind and caravan parks with the shutters down eight months of the year. So Ossay has this instead: an inland abyss, forty minutes’ walk from a Co-op, deeper than most of the sea anybody in the town has ever swum in. People drive a long way to get into it. That has always struck Sabine as the honest part. Nobody comes to the Cut for the scenery. There isn’t any. You come because it is deep and because it is close, in the way that people come to a certain kind of house on a certain kind of street, and everyone involved understands the transaction.
Her sister finds her at half past ten, which means she has been in the hut watching her through the window for an hour and a half deciding how to open.
“Good turnout,” he says.
“Eleven.”
“Eleven’s good for a Tuesday.” Maude has a folder under her arm and she is being careful not to look at it. “Sabine. The report.”

The man who holds the lease on the Cut has never once stood on this platform. He holds a licence to charge people to get into water he does not own, from a council that would prefer not to think about it, and he administers it from an office in a town twenty miles away, and he has spent two years asking the company that insures the site to reduce what he pays them. The company that insures the site employs Maude Vasseur to assess risk. That is the whole of the machinery and there is nobody in it who has ever put a hand in this water except the two of them.
“You’ll have it.”
“I know I’ll have it. I’m asking what’s in it.”
“Then wait five days and read it.”

He laughs the way men laugh when they have decided to be pleasant about something for exactly one more exchange. “The thing is,” he says, “the last one. The last person who did this job. He wrote nine pages about the walls.”
“The walls are undercut in three places.”

“The walls have been undercut since before I was born. Nobody dives the walls, they dive the line. Nine pages.” He shifts the folder. “And the insurer read nine pages about the walls and put the number up by a third, and I paid it, because what am I going to do. And this year they’ve said they want somebody who actually dives, not a surveyor. They said get a diver. So I got the best diver in the department.”
“I don’t dive.”
“You coach.”
“That’s not the same sentence.”

“It’s near enough for the form.” He says it lightly and it is the first cruel thing he has said, and she can see him decide to leave it there rather than sharpen it, which is worse. “Look. All I’m asking is that the report is about what happens in the water and not about the geology. That’s not me leaning. That’s me saying you’re the only person they’d believe.”
Sabine looks out at the Cut.

At this hour the surface is the colour of an unwashed window. The walls go straight down into it and there is a line where the slate stops being slate and starts being the reflection of slate, and then a little below that line the reflection gives up and there is simply an edge, and past the edge nothing. From the platform you can see perhaps two metres down. On a bright still afternoon in June, three. It looks like the top of something rather than the surface of it.
“They’d believe me,” she says.
“You know they would.”
“Maude, they’d believe me because of a thing that happened here nine years ago. That’s the whole of it. That’s the entire reason my name is worth anything to an insurer. You understand that.”
Maude has the decency to take a moment.
“Yes,” he says.
“All right.”
“That’s not why I asked.”
“It’s why they’ll believe me.”

“Yes.” He puts the folder down on the rail, and does not open it, and looks at the water with her for a while, and out of what is either respect or fear he does not say the name. Nobody in Ossay says the name to her. It has been nine years and the town has arranged itself very carefully around a gap.

Down on the water the woman who came up at eleven past nine is going again. Sabine watches her do the breathe-up: face down, arms out, the long slow emptying that looks from a distance like a person asleep on the surface of a puddle. Her safety diver hangs beside her with a hand on her shoulder blade, and when she rolls to go he takes the hand away and says something Sabine can’t hear, and the woman folds at the waist and is gone.

The line goes taut. That is the only sign. One thin rope running from a buoy down into the dark with a weight on the end of it, and for the next two minutes the only evidence that there is a person in the world under that buoy is that the rope is slightly less slack than it was.
“I’ll write about the water,” Sabine says.

She waits until the last car has gone at four and the light has begun to go with it, and then she walks down the ramp to the water’s edge, which she does most days, and squats, and puts her right hand in.
The cold comes up through her wrist like a note being struck.

This is where the body remembers. Not the chest — everyone assumes it is the chest, and it isn’t. It is the face and the hands. There are nerves in the skin of the face that have been waiting, in every human being who ever lived, for cold water, and when the cold arrives they throw a switch that has nothing to do with what anyone wants. The heart slows. Not gently. It drops away like a lift with the cable cut and then catches somewhere down in the twenties and walks. Four seconds between beats. Long enough that the first time it happens to a person they surface convinced they are dying, and the second time they surface convinced they have found religion. The blood leaves the hands and the feet and gathers in the middle where it is needed. The chest fills.

None of it is voluntary. That is the part she has never been able to teach properly, though she has said it a thousand times in a hundred different ways. You do not do the switch. The switch is done to you. All any diver ever gets to decide is whether to be in the water when it happens.
She holds her hand under until it stops hurting and starts belonging to somebody else, and counts, and at nineteen she feels her own pulse go long in her throat, and she takes the hand out.

Nine years. Her coat is dry. Her hair is dry. She has not put her face in this water since the fourth of April nine years ago, and she has stood at the edge of it four hundred times, and every single time she has put a hand in and taken it out again, and there is no version of this she can explain to anyone, including Maude, especially Maude, who has been trying to get her to explain it for most of a decade and who is under the impression that it is guilt.
It isn’t guilt. Guilt would be easier. Guilt is a thing you can carry up a hill.
Sabine dries her hand on her coat, and looks at the black, and the black does what it always does, which is nothing at all, patiently.

Then she goes up to the hut and signs herself off the site for the day, and on the way out she notices that one of the eleven cars is still in the gravel: an old estate, mud to the sills, a wetsuit hung over the open tailgate steaming very slightly in the cold.
She stops.
She looks back at the water. From up here, in this light, you cannot see the buoy.
She stands in the gravel for a long moment with her keys in her hand, and then she puts them back in her pocket and walks down the ramp again.
TWO. 3 METRES
Nobody is in the water. That is the first thing she establishes, and it takes her ninety seconds of standing at the edge in the failing light to establish it, and it does not make her feel better.

The buoy sits where it sits. The line goes down out of it and disappears at a hand’s depth. There is no diver on the surface and no diver hanging at three metres doing the slow thing beginners do, and there is nobody on the platform to say he went that way, because it is twenty past four on a Tuesday in Ossay and everyone with any sense has gone to get warm.
Then the surface breaks eight metres out from the ramp and a man comes up, and he is not gasping either.

He takes three breaths, small then larger then larger, and turns his head and sees her, and there is a fractional pause while he decides how much trouble he is in. Then he swims in with an easy sideways stroke, one arm, unhurried, and gets a hand on the concrete lip of the ramp.
“You’re Sabine Vasseur,” he says.
“You’re on your own.”
“I know.”
“There’s a rule.”
“I know the rule.”

He is somewhere in his middle twenties. Black hair flattened to his skull, three days of beard, a nose that has been broken once and set by somebody in a hurry. His lips have gone the colour lips go. He is shivering in the small tight way of a man who has been cold for an hour and has stopped noticing, and he is looking at her with what she recognises immediately and with some annoyance as delight.
“How deep,” she says.
“Not deep.”
“How deep.”
“Thirty-one.”
She lets a beat go. “There’s a woman who did thirty-one this morning with a safety diver on her shoulder and a stopwatch and a rope she could hold. She’s been diving nine years.”
“I know. She’s good.” He says it without any edge at all, as a fact he is glad about. “I wasn’t on the line. I don’t like the line.”
“You don’t like the line.”
“It gets in the way.”

Sabine crouches on the ramp so that her face is at the level of his, which is a thing she does with beginners in a pool and has not done outdoors in nine years, and she is aware that she is doing it and cannot make herself stop.

“The single rule,” she says, “the only one, the one that comes before every other rule in this sport, is that you do not do it alone. Not because you might drown. You’re not going to drown, you’re too good to drown. Because at some point, and it will be at a depth you’ve done fifty times before, the lights are going to go out. Not dim. Out. And you will get no warning at all, and the last thing you’ll remember is feeling fine.” She holds up one finger. “Ten seconds. That’s the window. Ten seconds where somebody who is already touching you gets your face out of the water, and if they do, you come round and you’re embarrassed. If nobody’s touching you—”
“I know.”
“Then say the rest of it.”
He looks at her. Then, obediently, as though it were a poem he had been made to learn: “Then the mouth opens by itself, and it isn’t drowning yet, but it’s the last part before drowning.”
Something goes through her that she does not have a name for.
“Who taught you that.”
“Nobody taught me anything,” he says. “I read.”

His name is Aurel Nizan and he has been coming to the Cut for fourteen months, which is a thing she can verify and does, later, from the sign-in book, where his name appears in a slanting hand ninety-one times. He works nights at the plastics works on the Ossay road, four on and four off, which means his diving is done on weekday afternoons in the empty hours, which means for fourteen months there has been a man in this water almost entirely unobserved.

He does not seem furtive about it. That is what unsettles her most, walking back up to the hut with him talking beside her, both of them steaming faintly in the cold. He is not sneaking. He has simply found something and gone at it, alone, in a hole outside a town of four thousand people, with no coach and no club and no safety diver, out of books, and he has got himself to thirty-one metres.
“How long can you hold it,” she asks.
“On the surface? Five twenty.”
“Say the number again.”

“Five minutes and twenty seconds. Lying face down, not moving.” He shrugs and immediately regrets the shrug, because his shoulders are locked with cold. “It’s not a good number. There’s a man who does eleven.”
“There is one man in the recorded history of this sport who does eleven and he doesn’t work nights at a plastics works.”
Aurel laughs. It is a good laugh, unguarded, and it goes out flat across the water and comes back off the slate half a second later.

She should report him. There is a line on the form for it: breaches observed. There is even a procedure — a written warning, then a suspension of access, then a letter to the council. The lease-holder would sign it from twenty miles away without reading it, because a solo diver is an uninsured death waiting to happen on land he pays for and never visits.

She does not report him. She writes, in the log, 31m unaccompanied, verbal warning given, diver receptive, which is two-thirds true, and she closes the book, and she goes home and does not sleep well.

On Thursday she teaches, because it is Thursday, and there are five of them on the shallow shelf at the western end where the old cutting bench sits three metres under and gives you a floor to stand on.

Two sisters in their thirties who have booked the course as a birthday thing and are already, she can see, going to be adequate and content and never come back. A man called Petar who is too strong, which is the commonest problem in the sport and the hardest to talk anybody out of. A boy of nineteen who has been sent by his father. And a woman in her fifties who has been diving nine years, does not need the session, and comes to the sessions anyway.
“Face in the water,” Sabine says. “All of you. Don’t hold your breath. I want you to just put your face in and breathe out slowly through your nose and count to twenty.”
They do it. Petar does it too fast and comes up first.
“Again. Slower.”
They do it again.
“Now. Hands up if your heart slowed down.”
Nobody puts a hand up, because nobody can tell, because you almost never can from the outside.

“It did,” Sabine says. “All five of you. Every one of you just had your heart rate drop, and you didn’t feel it, and you couldn’t have stopped it if you’d wanted to. There are nerves in the skin of your face, here—” she draws a line with two fingers, across her own cheekbones and along the ridge of her brow, “—that have been sitting in your head your entire life waiting to be touched by cold water. That’s all they’re for. And when they get touched, a switch goes, and your heart slows down, and the blood goes out of your hands and feet and gathers up in the middle of you where it’s actually useful.”
“Why,” says one of the sisters.

“Because we used to live in it.” Sabine says this the way she always says it, flatly, because the flatness is what makes it land. “Every animal that goes in and out of water has this. Seals have it, obviously. Beavers have it. So do we, and we didn’t earn it, we just never lost it, and it means that a human being who has never dived in her life is already built for it and doesn’t know.”
The boy of nineteen has stopped looking bored.

“That’s the switch,” she says. “You’ll hear people call it other things. Ignore them. It’s the switch, it’s free, it’s the whole reason any of this is possible, and here is the important part.” She waits until she has all five. “You don’t do it. It is done to you. You can make it come on faster and harder with practice, and you can make it come on faster by getting the cold on your face early, and that’s most of what training is. But you never do it. The only decision you ever get to make in this entire sport is whether you’re in the water when it happens.”

The woman in her fifties, treading beside the bench, catches her eye and looks away, and Sabine understands that she has heard this said thirty times and has noticed, this time, that it was said differently.

She keeps them shallow. Three metres, the bench under their feet, twenty-five minutes, and then she takes them out because the two sisters have gone the grey-white that means the cold has got past the suit and into the meat, and cold is not a discomfort, cold is a bill. A cold diver burns through everything faster. A cold diver shivers, and shivering is expensive, and the expense comes off the only account that matters.
Petar wants to know when they can go to the line.
“You’ve been in the water four hours total,” Sabine says. “The line’s still going to be here.”
“Other people are on the line.”
“Other people have four thousand hours in this water.”
Petar wants to argue. She lets him not argue, which is a technique, and while he is not arguing she is looking past his shoulder at the far end of the Cut where the buoy sits.
The line is taut.

It has been taut for — she does not know how long. She has been teaching. She looks at her watch, which is useless, and then at the buoy, and she counts, and at forty-one the surface breaks beside it and a dark head comes up and takes three breaths, small then larger then larger.
Nobody is with him.

Petar is still talking. Sabine says, “Excuse me a moment,” in a voice that stops him mid-word, and walks the length of the shelf to the eastern end with her hands in her pockets, and stands, and waits, and watches Aurel Nizan tread water at the buoy for four minutes doing absolutely nothing that a person unfamiliar with the sport would find alarming.

He is not resting. She knows the difference. He is holding his position, and his head is turned so that he is looking down and slightly to his left, at nothing, at forty metres of water and then fifty more, with the loose attention of a man on a station platform waiting for a train that he knows is coming and is not late.
Then he lifts his head, and sees her on the shelf, and raises a hand.
Not a wave. Thumb and forefinger, a circle, held up.
I’m okay.

She does not raise a hand back. She stands there with the cold coming up off the water and she thinks, with a clarity that will bother her for weeks, that she has just been told something by a man who has no idea he told her anything, in a language that she and one other person are the only ones ever to have spoken in this water.
He grins at her across forty metres of surface, and folds, and goes down again.
THREE. 5 METRES
From the log of Aurel Nizan. Fourth notebook, unnumbered pages, written in pencil.
Red is the first colour to die and it dies at five metres.

I want to put that down properly because when I tell people they think I mean it gets dark. It doesn’t get dark at five metres. At five metres on a decent day it’s bright enough to read a newspaper. What happens is that the water takes the red out of the light, the way a filter would, except a filter takes something out of what you see and this takes something out of what exists. There is no red down there to be seen. It isn’t hiding. It has been removed.

So: the O-ring on my mask strap is red. In the car park it is red. At two metres it is a dull red, like brick. At five metres it is grey. Not greyish. Grey, exactly and completely, the same grey as the strap it sits on, and I can hold it up in front of my face in good light and know perfectly well that it is red and be entirely unable to make it be red.

Orange goes next, at about ten. Then yellow, around twenty, and yellow going is the one you notice, because yellow is what most of the light has been by then, and when it goes the whole hole changes character in about four metres. Green holds out longest. Green gets you to thirty.
After that it is blue for a while, and then it is not blue.

I have written blue in this notebook eleven times in fourteen months and every one of them is a lie of convenience. What is down there past thirty-five is not a colour. The closest I have come to it: shut your eyes in a dark room and keep them shut for longer than is comfortable, twenty minutes, half an hour, until you have stopped waiting for anything. What’s there then isn’t black. There’s a field. It moves slightly. It has a grain to it, like the grain on a photograph pushed too far, and it has no source, because your eyes are closed and nothing is getting in.
That is what is in the Cut past thirty-five metres. That exact thing, at scale, with your eyes open.

The first time I understood that I had to come up. I did it wrong and got the shakes on the surface and had nobody with me, which I know, and I am putting it in the notebook because I said at the start that I would put everything in the notebook.

I gave up the spearfishing in the second month and I want to write down why, because I have not said it out loud to anybody and if I say it out loud it will come out sounding like a conversion and it isn’t one.

I started with a gun, because that is how men my age start. You get a cheap gun and a snorkel and you go to that awful coast four hours away and you hang around in three metres of surge waiting for something stupid to swim past, and you shoot at it, and you miss, and the missing is most of it, and it is a good enough way to spend a Saturday.
The reason it works, the actual reason, is that it gives you an errand. You cannot hold your breath for two minutes as a project.

Nobody can. Try it dry in a chair sometime and you will find that the seconds have edges on them and you will be aware of every single one. But go under with an errand — with a thing you are looking for, a gully you want to see round, a fish you have decided is yours — and the seconds stop having edges. You come up and it’s been ninety seconds and you’d have sworn it was thirty. The errand does that. The errand is a machine for making time not exist.
So I got very good at holding my breath by accident, while I was busy doing something else, which is how everybody gets good at everything.
And then in the second month, in the Cut, in maybe eight metres of water on the shelf, I put the gun down on the bench because it was in my way, and went down without it.

I do not have a good way of writing what happened next because nothing happened. That is the whole content of it. Nothing happened for about forty seconds and it was the most substantial forty seconds I have ever been present for.
No errand. Nothing to look for, nothing to be pointing at, nothing to want. Just a man in cold grey water with his lungs shut and his heart going once every four seconds and nowhere at all to be.

I have spent my entire life in an argument with myself. I don’t say that for sympathy, I say it as a description of the weather. There is a voice and it has opinions about everything I do while I am doing it, and about everything I did years ago while I am trying to sleep, and I have tried the things people try. I have tried drink, which works for ninety minutes and then charges interest. I have tried running until I was sick. I have tried a course of tablets that made the voice quieter and made everything else quieter too, so that I was fine, and nothing was interesting, and I stopped taking them without telling the doctor, which was stupid.
Under the water on the bench in the second month the voice stopped.

Not quieter. Stopped. There was no argument, because there was no one to argue with, because the thing that does the arguing had put itself down along with the gun. And what was left was — I want to be careful here — not peace. Peace suggests a good feeling and this was not a feeling. It was more like the removal of a noise you had forgotten was a noise. A room where a fridge has been unplugged.
I came up and I sat on the bench with my head out and I was shaking, and it was not the cold.
I sold the gun that week.

I have read everything I can find and most of it is written for people who want to compete, and I don’t. There is a whole apparatus — the federations, the judges, the ratified attempts, the cards you hand up from the plate at the bottom to prove you got there. None of that is anything to me. I don’t want a number on a website. I want the fridge unplugged and I want it for longer.
But the literature is useful in one particular way and I want to record the useful thing because it changed how I do this.
I had assumed, like everybody assumes, that the reason you have to come up is that you are running out of air.
It isn’t.

The desperation — the thing that makes you claw for the surface, the thing that feels exactly like drowning — is not about running low. It is about waste. Your body makes a gas as it works, and that gas builds up, and there are sensors that watch the level of it, and when the level gets high they set off an alarm, and the alarm is the most convincing thing you will ever experience. It is not a suggestion. It is an absolute, screaming, total certainty that you must breathe now.
And it is not measuring the thing that can kill you.

The waste gas builds up on a timetable and the air runs down on a different timetable, and in a trained person those two timetables come apart. Which means the alarm goes off long before there is any danger — and it also means that the alarm can be over and done with, silent, finished, while the danger is still coming.

You can learn to ignore it. That is the entire skill. There is nothing else in this sport. Everything else is fins and technique and equalising your ears. The skill is that a man can be taught to hear his own body screaming that it is dying and to file the screaming as noise.
I read that and I put the book down and I went and stood in the kitchen for a while.

Because if it can be done with that alarm — the oldest one, the one that comes before language, the one that every animal has and no animal ignores — then what exactly is the status of all the other ones. I have alarms about my job, about money, about the woman I lived with for three years and the way it ended, about the fact that I am twenty-six and work nights in a building that makes plastic clips for a company that makes plastic clips. What if those are all the same class of object. What if they are all measuring the wrong thing and going off on a timetable of their own, and the only reason I have never been able to file them as noise is that nobody ever told me I was allowed to.
The books do not go into that. The books are about fins.
I have got to thirty-one metres.

I did it four times last week and the fourth time was better than the first, which is not how it is supposed to work — you get worse across a session, that’s the rule, the debt accumulates — and I don’t know what to make of that yet so I am putting it down without a conclusion.
I know I am supposed to have somebody with me. I have read every version of the argument and I agree with all of it, and when I am on land I fully intend to sort it out.

The difficulty is that there is nobody. There is a club forty miles away that meets on Sundays when I am on nights. There is a woman who comes on Thursdays who is good and who is kind and who dives with her husband. There is a coach who comes out to the Cut on Thursdays and teaches beginners on the shelf and has apparently not been in the water herself for years, and who has watched me twice now from the concrete with her hands in her pockets, and who I have not worked out at all.
Something else, and this is the last thing and then I’ll stop.
At thirty-one metres, at the deepest part of it, in that grey field with no source — the seconds have gone back to not having edges. And I have not got an errand.
Which means something is doing the job the errand used to do.

I don’t know what. I am not going to invent something. But I have started noticing that I am attending down there, the way you attend when somebody is in the room, and I am aware that this is exactly what the literature says happens to people who are cold and alone and running low in the dark, and that it has a boring name, and that everyone it has ever happened to has believed at the time that theirs was different.
Mine is probably not different.
I am going deeper on Thursday.
FOUR. 10 METRES
“I’ll dive with you,” Sabine says.

It is the following Thursday and it is raining in the flat determined way it rains on the moor, and Aurel is standing on the ramp in a half-peeled wetsuit with his arms out of the sleeves and the top folded down at his waist, and he has just come up from twenty-eight metres alone for the second time that afternoon, and she has been standing there watching him do it, and she is as surprised as he is.
“You don’t dive,” he says.
“I’ll be your safety. That’s not the same sentence.”
He looks at her for a moment too long. Then, because he is twenty-six and cannot help it: “Why?”

“Because you’re going to keep going down there whether I’m on the surface or not, and if you do it alone you will die in that water this year, and I’d rather not.” She hears how it comes out. “Also because the man who holds the lease has asked me to write a report about how safe this hole is, and I can’t very well write it while there’s someone getting to thirty metres in it on his own four days a week.”
“So I’m a liability.”
“You’re a liability.”
“That’s honest.”
“It’s a third of it,” she says.

He waits for the other two thirds. She does not give them to him. What she does instead is hold out her hand for his mask, and when he hands it over she turns it in her fingers and looks at the strap, which is the wrong sort, and at the skirt, which is perished at one corner and will start letting water in within the month, and she gives it back.
“Sunday,” she says. “You’re not on nights Sunday.”
“How do you know what I’m on?”
“You sign a book.”
She takes him down to ten metres and keeps him there for an hour and he hates it.

This is deliberate and it is also the only honest thing she can do with him, because a diver who has taught himself out of books to thirty-one metres has one particular hole in him, always, in the same place, and the hole is not courage or technique. It is that he has never once had somebody watch him closely enough to tell him what he actually does.
“Again,” she says. “And this time when you turn, look at me.”
“I did look at you.”
“You looked at the line.”
“I don’t use the line.”
“You looked at where the line would be if you used it.”

He goes down again. Ten metres, a slow drift to the bench, hang, turn, come up. She holds at five with her face out, watching the shape of him coming up out of the grey, and she is not diving, she is floating on the surface in a wetsuit with her head above the water and one arm hooked through the buoy strap, and that is what she has agreed to and she has made it clear that it is what she has agreed to.
He surfaces. Three breaths. Mask off. Eyes. Circle. “I’m okay.”
“Better,” she says. “You’re kicking on the way down.”
“I have to get down.”

“You have to get down for the first twelve metres. After that you’ll go on your own. Everybody knows that and everybody kicks anyway, and every kick you make in the first thirty seconds you pay for at the bottom with interest.” She wipes rain off her face, which is pointless. “It’s not about strength. Nothing here is about strength. The whole sport is arithmetic and you are the only variable that spends.”
“How much.”
“How much what?”
“How much does a kick cost.”

And there it is: the actual question, asked plainly, by a man who wants the real answer and not the encouraging one, and Sabine feels the thing she has not felt in nine years and has been careful not to name, which is the pleasure of having something to give somebody who wants it.
“Come out,” she says. “I’ll draw it for you.”
They sit in the hut with the heater going and two cups of tea and a page from the back of the sign-in book, and she draws him two lines.

“This,” she says, “is what you’ve got. Air. It goes down at a rate. The rate depends on how hard you’re working, how cold you are, how frightened you are, and how deep you are. It only ever goes down. When it gets to here—” she taps the bottom of the page, “—the lights go out. No warning. You’ll feel excellent. That’s not a joke and it’s not a figure of speech, that is the documented thing: people feel good in the last ten seconds. Then nothing.”
“All right.”

“Now this.” A second line, starting low, climbing. “This is the waste. Your body makes it while it works and there’s nowhere for it to go, so it builds. And the alarm — the thing that makes you want to breathe, the thing that feels like dying — is watching this line. Not the other one. This one.”
Aurel is very still.

“So,” Sabine says. “The urge to breathe is a lie. It’s not lying about whether it’s uncomfortable, it’s absolutely honest about that. It’s lying about what it’s measuring. It tells you you’re about to die and what it actually knows is that there’s rubbish piling up in a corner.”
“I read that.”

“Then you read the first half.” She puts the pencil down. “Here’s the second half, and this is the part the books do a bad job of, and it’s the reason I’m sitting in a hut with you instead of writing you up.

“You can train the alarm. Everyone can. Two weeks of work and it comes later and quieter, and after a few years it comes so late that it’s barely an event. And people describe that as getting stronger. It isn’t. Nothing about you got stronger. You just turned down a bell.” She taps the first line, the one going down. “This one never changes. This one has no bell on it at all. It never did. There is no sensation anywhere in the human body for the thing that actually kills freedivers.

“So what training does — what I would be doing to you, if I take you on — is not make you safer. It removes the only warning you had, which was never a warning about the right thing, and it replaces it with arithmetic and a person on the surface. That’s it.
That’s the whole of the safety in this sport. Sums, and somebody watching.”
The rain goes on the roof of the hut.
“That’s a bleak way to put it,” Aurel says.

“It’s the accurate way to put it. I’ve found that people who are told the bleak version early tend to be alive later.” She drinks some tea. “You’ll want to go deeper than thirty-one. You’ll go, whatever I say. So we’ll do it with the sums.”
“And somebody watching.”
“And somebody watching.”

He turns the page round and looks at the two lines, the one falling and the one climbing, and where they cross, and he says, not to her: “So the feeling is real and it’s about the wrong thing, and you can be taught to stop listening to it, and nothing takes its place.”
“Yes.”
“How much of everything is like that?”
Sabine, who has spent nine years standing at the edge of cold water putting one hand in, says: “Drink your tea.”

Maude arrives at twenty past three with a laptop bag over her shoulder and rain on her glasses, which is how Sabine knows she has walked from the road rather than driven in, which is how Sabine knows this is not a social call and is meant to look like one.
“They’ve hired you,” Maude says.
“Hello, Maude.”
“My company has hired you to write a water safety assessment on the Cut.”
“He has.”
“For the insurer.”
“For the insurer.”

Maude stands in the doorway of the hut and does not come in. She is three years younger than Sabine and looks five years older, which is a thing she achieved deliberately somewhere in her thirties and wears like a coat. Behind the wet glasses her eyes go once round the hut: the heater, the two cups, the page from the sign-in book with two lines drawn on it, the young man sitting on the bench in a half-peeled wetsuit who has stopped moving.
“And who’s this,” Maude says.
“Aurel Nizan.”
“He dives here.”
“He does.”

“On his own.” Maude has not looked at the sign-in book and does not need to; she has been reading sign-in books at the Cut for nine years, and Sabine understands, in that moment, with a lurch, that Maude has been reading that particular name for months. “Ninety-one times, mostly weekday afternoons. Nobody with him. I flagged it in March.”
“You flagged it to who?”

“To the lease-holder. Who did nothing, because a man who dives alone four times a week is the most profitable customer he has, and because he has never been here.” Maude finally comes in, and puts the laptop bag down, and takes her glasses off, and she looks at Aurel with an expression that Sabine has seen her use on claimants. “Mr Nizan. I’m Maude Vasseur. I assess risk for the company that insures this site. Would you tell me the deepest you’ve been in this water?”
Aurel looks at Sabine.
“Don’t look at her,” Maude says pleasantly. “She’s not your solicitor.”
“Thirty-one metres.”
“Alone.”
“Yes.”
“Thank you.” Maude sits down, and opens the laptop, and does not turn it on. “Sabine. Outside.”
They stand in the rain at the top of the ramp, which is as far as Maude will go, because Maude does not go down the ramp.
“You cannot be his coach,” Maude says.
“I’m his safety.”
“You cannot be his anything. You are writing a report that says this water is safe, and the insurer is going to read it, and you have a documented interest in—”
“Say the sentence, Maude.”
“—in the water being safe,” Maude finishes, evenly. “That’s the sentence. That’s the whole sentence. Don’t do that thing where you dare me.”
Sabine looks out at the Cut. In the rain the surface has no shine on it at all; it takes the rain and gives back nothing, so that from up here the hole reads as a piece missing out of the moor.

“He’s going to do it anyway,” she says. “You know he is. You’ve had his name since March. You could have written to the council in March and had him barred and you didn’t, and you didn’t because you knew exactly what you know now, which is that a man like that gets barred from the Cut and drives to a reservoir and goes in off a bank with nobody within a mile of him. Barring him kills him. So don’t stand in the rain and tell me about interests.”
Maude is quiet for a moment.
“Nine years,” she says.
“Don’t.”

“Nine years you haven’t put your face in that water, and this week you got a wetsuit out.” Maude puts her glasses back on. “I’ve stopped expecting you to tell me what happened. I’ve genuinely stopped, Sabine, it’s been a relief, you should try it. But I want you to hear me say this once so it’s said. I know what you look like when you’ve decided something and are going to let it happen slowly. You’ve had that face since you were fifteen.”
“He’s twenty-six years old and he taught himself out of books and he’s better already than I was at thirty.”
“That’s not a reassurance. Do you hear that that’s not a reassurance?”
Sabine says nothing.

Down at the bottom of the ramp Aurel has come out of the hut with his wetsuit peeled to the waist and steam coming off his shoulders in the cold, and he is standing at the water’s edge in the rain, not going in, looking down. He crouches. He puts his right hand in, past the wrist.
Sabine watches him do it and feels the floor of her chest go out from under her.

He holds it there. He is counting; she can see him counting. And at about nineteen his shoulders drop a fraction, the way they do when the throat goes long, and he takes the hand out and shakes it and stands up.
“What,” says Maude.
“Nothing,” says Sabine.
FIVE. 0 METRES
The first thing Sabine gives him is a sheet of paper, and he is visibly disappointed, which she enjoys.
“That’s homework.”
“I can see it’s homework.”
“You thought I was going to take you deep.”
“I thought we’d be in the water,” Aurel says.

“You’ll be in the water on Sunday for an hour and you’ll be on that sofa for nine hours between now and then, and the sofa is where you’ll actually get better.” She taps the sheet. “Everybody hates this part. I hate this part. It’s the part that works.”
The sheet has two sets of numbers on it and she makes him read them in front of her, out loud, which is a technique.

“First one,” she says. “You hold your breath for two minutes. Then you rest for two minutes. Then you hold for two minutes again, and rest for a minute forty. Then two minutes, rest a minute twenty. And so on down. Eight rounds. The hold never changes. The rest gets shorter every time.”
“So it gets harder.”

“It gets harder because you’re starting each one with more rubbish in you than the last.” Sabine sits back. “That table doesn’t make you fitter. It doesn’t buy you a single second. All it does is make you meet the alarm, eight times in an hour, in a room, with nothing at stake. You get to be screamed at by your own body while sitting on a sofa in your own house where you are in absolutely no danger, and after enough of that the screaming stops being an event.”
“And the second table?”

“Opposite. The rest is always the same and the hold gets longer. Two minutes, then two ten, then two twenty, all the way up until you can’t.” She shrugs. “That one teaches you to be poor. To run low and keep functioning while you’re low. The first one teaches you to put up with the alarm. The second teaches you to work with an empty account.”
Aurel looks at the sheet. “Which is more important?”

“The first one keeps you comfortable. The second one is the one that kills people, because it teaches you to be very good at being nearly out.” She says it flatly, in the tone she keeps for the bleak version. “You need both. And you need to write down every single round, including the ones you gave up on, especially the ones you gave up on, because a table with no failures in it is a table somebody’s lying about.”
He does them and he does them properly and this is where she starts finding out who he is, which is what the dry work is actually for.

She has never told anybody that. There is a whole coaching literature about the physical purpose of the tables and it is accurate and it is not why she sets them. Anybody can be brave in water once. Water does most of the work — it is cold and dark and interesting, and a person with something to prove will go a long way into it on adrenaline alone and feel wonderful afterwards.
Nobody feels wonderful doing table work.

It is done alone, in a room, in ordinary clothes, on a Tuesday, with a phone propped against a mug for a timer. It is uncomfortable and dull and there is no scenery and nothing to look at and nobody watching, and it takes an hour, and it has to be done four times a week for the rest of your diving life, and it never gets more interesting.
So the tables tell you the only thing about a diver that matters, which is what they do when it is boring.

She has had eighty-one divers. Sixty of them stopped doing the tables within a month and lied about it for a while and then stopped lying. Fifteen did them in bursts, heroically, for a fortnight, and then not at all. Six did them.
Aurel does them at four in the morning.
That is the detail she cannot let go of.

He works nights. Four on, four off, at the plastics works on the Ossay road, six in the evening until six in the morning, and he comes off shift at six and drives home and eats something and does an hour of table work at seven in the morning with the curtains shut before he sleeps.

He shows her the book. Every round, every date, every failure — and there are failures, plenty of them, marked with a small dash and a note. Gave up r6. Gave up r7, r8. Bad night. Nearly threw up. He has not tidied it. He has not made himself look better anywhere in it.
“This is four weeks,” she says.
“Four and a bit.”
“You haven’t missed one.”
“No.”
“Why not?”
Aurel thinks about it. He always thinks about it, and she has stopped finding that charming and started finding it informative.
“Because it’s the only thing I’ve ever been given to do that has a right answer,” he says.
The rest of the dry work is worse and she gives him all of it in the second week.

The bowl. A washing-up bowl of cold water on the kitchen table, and he puts his face in it and holds. That is the whole exercise and it looks, and is, ridiculous. The switch lives in the skin of the face, and it can be trained, and it can be trained on land in a kitchen, and the more often you make it happen the sooner and harder it comes when you actually need it. She tells him to add ice.

He tells her, in the third week, that he does it at four in the morning after the tables, and that the neighbour’s dog barks when the tap runs at that hour, and that he has started using water he put in the fridge the previous evening.
“You’re keeping a jug of cold water in the fridge to put your face in.”
“Yes.”
“Do you understand how that would sound to a person?”
“There’s nobody to say it to,” Aurel says.

The stretching. This is the one that takes the longest and hurts the most and produces the least visible result. A chest that is going to be squeezed to a fifth of its size needs to be a chest that can be squeezed. Ribs, the muscle sheet underneath, the whole cage. A stiff diver is a diver who tears something at sixty metres, and almost every man who comes to this sport is stiff, because almost every man who comes to this sport has spent his life making himself hard in the front.
She gives him four positions and he is appalling at all of them.

That is the first honest pleasure she has had in nine years — watching a young man who can hold his breath for five and a half minutes fail completely at lying on the floor and letting his ribs move. He is furious about it. He is furious in a quiet flat way that she recognises, and she works him at it for forty minutes twice a week for a month, on the concrete, in the rain, and it is the only part of the training he complains about.
“This isn’t diving,” he says, face down on a mat in the drizzle.
“No. This is the bill for diving, paid early.”
The breathe-up. Two minutes of doing nothing, correctly.

That is all it is. Face down on the surface, arms out, breathing slowly and completely out. And it is the hardest single thing she teaches anybody, and she teaches it last, because it cannot be done by effort and everything else in the sport can.
“You’re trying,” she tells him, on the surface, in June. “I can see you trying from here. You’re doing relaxation the way you do the tables.”
“How am I supposed to do it?”
“You’re not supposed to do it.”
“That’s not instruction. That’s a fortune cookie.”
Sabine laughs — properly, out loud, across the water, and hears it come back off the slate half a second later, and is briefly appalled at herself.

“All right,” she says. “Here’s the instruction. Relaxation in this sport is not a mood and it is not a state of mind and it has nothing whatever to do with being calm. It is a measurable physical condition. It means: no muscle in your body is doing anything it hasn’t been asked to do. That’s it. That’s the whole definition. A jaw that’s slightly set is spending. A hand that’s slightly closed is spending. A shoulder up round your ear because the water’s four degrees is spending, and you’ll pay for it at sixty metres in a currency you can’t see the balance of.
“So don’t relax. Go through yourself, part by part, and find what’s switched on that doesn’t need to be, and switch it off. It’s an inventory. It’s plumbing.”
He is quiet for a moment, treading.
“That’s the first thing anybody’s ever said to me about calming down that made any sense,” he says.
She writes it all down, every session, every table, every failure, in a hardback book she bought in April for that purpose and has told nobody about.

What she is recording, if anybody ever asks — and somebody will, eventually, and it will be her sister — is a training programme that is conservative to the point of timidity. Six weeks before she let him past forty metres, when he was at thirty-one when she met him. Depth increases of five metres, never eight. Two rest days a week enforced. Homework logged. Stretching. Every single thing correct, every single thing defensible, every page signed and dated at the bottom in her own hand.
She has been coaching for twenty-two years and she has never once signed a training page.
She is not entirely sure, in the second week of May, who she thinks is going to read it.

But she knows the reason she started, and the reason is that on the twenty-sixth of April a young man came up out of that water and said six words to her on the surface, and every single thing she has done since has been done in the presence of those six words, and there is a version of what she is doing that would look, written down by somebody else, extremely bad.
So she writes it down herself.
That way it is a record.
If she stopped writing it down, it would be a secret.
SIX. 10 METRES
There is one skill in this sport that cannot be got at by wanting it, and it stops nearly everybody, and it stopped him.
“Your ears,” Sabine says.
“My ears are fine.”

“Your ears are fine to thirty-one metres because you’re strong and because there was still something left in you to push with. There isn’t at fifty. That’s the wall. That’s the whole wall, and it’s got nothing to do with courage, and about half the people who come to this sport never get over it.”
They are on the concrete in the last week of April with the rain off and the light going, and she draws it for him on the back of a page from the sign-in book, because she draws everything.

Going down, the water squeezes the air spaces in a head. Behind the eardrum there is a small space and it has to be filled or the drum bends inward and eventually gives, and filling it means getting air up into it from below. Everyone knows this; everyone who has ever been on an aeroplane has done a version of it.
The version everyone does is: shut the mouth, pinch the nose, and push from the chest.

“And that works,” she says, “to about twenty metres, and then it stops working, and it stops working for a reason that has nothing to do with your technique. It stops working because there is nothing left in your chest to push with. By forty metres what you took down with you is a fifth of the size it was. You can push as hard as you like. There’s no volume there. You’re squeezing an empty bag.”
“So what do you do?”
“You stop using your chest. You move air with your tongue.”
It takes him eleven weeks and it is the only part of the training that ever makes him look defeated.

The skill is to take a small amount of air, hold it in the mouth and throat, seal it off from the lungs entirely, and then pump it upward using the back of the tongue like a piston. The lungs are not involved. The chest does not move. It is a completely separate mechanism from breathing, and almost nobody can do it the first hundred times they try, and the reason is that it requires the deliberate voluntary control of muscles that no human being has ever had to think about.
“It’s like being told to move your ears,” Aurel says, on the concrete, in May, after forty minutes of failing.
“It’s exactly like that. Some people can, most people can’t, and everybody can learn, and there’s no shortcut and no trick and nobody has ever found one in the whole history of the sport.”
“How long did it take you?”
“Fourteen weeks.”
He looks at her. “Fourteen.”
“I was twenty-two and I cried about it in a car park in Brest and I have told nobody that in twenty-two years.”
He laughs. She lets him.
The awful part is that he has been doing it wrong for fourteen months and getting away with it.
That is what she finds in the second week, and it is the first time she raises her voice at him.

He has taught himself, out of books, a hybrid — a bit of the tongue, a bit of the chest, done fast, done hard, and it has been working, and it has been working the way a bodged repair works, which is until it doesn’t. She makes him take it apart. She makes him go back to five metres, on the shelf, over the bench, and do it slowly, and it is humiliating, and he is a man who has been to thirty-one metres alone and is now being made to hover at five metres in a wetsuit going click, click, click with his tongue while a woman watches his face.
“This is the worst thing I’ve ever done,” he says.
“Good.”
“You’re enjoying it.”
“I’m enjoying it enormously,” Sabine says. “You’ve had fourteen months of nobody looking at you. This is what it’s like when somebody looks.”

And that, she thinks afterwards, driving home, is the whole of coaching. It is not knowledge. He had the knowledge; he read more than she has. It is that a person doing a difficult thing alone cannot see what they actually do, and will go on not seeing it for years, and the only cure is somebody standing close enough for long enough to say you are doing this, not that, and the strange violent intimacy of that is the reason people remember their coaches for the rest of their lives.
She has not done this for nine years.
She had forgotten she was good at it. That is not vanity. It is worse than vanity — it is that she had forgotten, and the forgetting had been comfortable, and the remembering is not.

The drill comes at the end of the third week and she does it on a Sunday when there is nobody else at the Cut, and she tells him what it is on the drive down and gives him the whole of it in the car park so that he cannot say afterwards that he was not warned.
“You’re going to practise being taken.”
“Being what?”

“You’re going to go limp in the water and let me get you out, and you’re going to do it about nine times, and you’re going to hate it.” She locks the car. “And then we’re going to do it the other way round.”
The four steps are simple and every diver on earth learns them and almost nobody ever uses them, and the ones who do use them use them once, badly, in a panic, on somebody they love.

Get the airway out of the water and keep it out. That comes before everything, before assessment, before shouting, before anything at all, because a person whose lights have gone out has perhaps ten seconds before the mouth opens by itself, and if the mouth opens above water they cough and come round and are embarrassed, and if it opens below water it is the beginning of the other thing.
Take the mask off.

Blow across the face. That is the actual instruction, and it sounds absurd until you know why: the cold on the face is the switch, and blowing air across wet skin is cold, and the switch is the last thing in a human being to stop working. You are not comforting them. You are ringing a bell in the only room that is still occupied.
And talk to them. Say their name and tell them to breathe, over and over, in an ordinary voice, to a person who is not there.
He is bad at going limp and good at everything else.

Nine times she tows him in, and nine times he cannot stop his neck from helping, and on the tenth she says, “You’re holding your own head up,” and he says, “I know,” and on the eleventh he stops doing it, and she gets a hand under his jaw and his weight comes onto her forearm entirely, all of it, the whole dead mass of a twenty-six-year-old man in four-degree water, and she tows him thirty metres to the ramp with his face out and his eyes shut and his mouth slightly open.
She takes his mask off. She blows across his face. She says: “Aurel. Breathe.”
And he opens his eyes.

They look at each other for slightly too long, at the bottom of a concrete ramp, in a hole in the moor, and then he says, “That’s horrible,” and she says, “Yes,” and neither of them says anything else about it.
Then she has to be the body.

She has thought about this for eleven days and she has structured the entire session so that it arrives last, and she has considered four different ways of not doing it, and every single one of them would be a coach declining to complete the standard drill, and if she declines it she has to write down why in a book she signs and dates.
So she gets in the water and swims out to the buoy and turns onto her back and shuts her eyes and lets go.

It takes her three attempts. Twice she comes up on her own, spluttering, furious with herself, and the third time she gets it — everything off, everything switched out, the inventory done, the whole plumbing of her shut down deliberately for the first time in nine years — and she lies on the surface of the Cut with her face half under and her ears full of water and no muscle in her body doing anything it has not been asked to do.
And she hears, from a long way off, muffled, the sound of a young man coming through the water towards her.
Then a hand comes under her jaw.
Her face lifts clear. Her mask comes off — his hands are quick and careful and he does not fumble it. Cold air moves across her wet skin, deliberately, from a mouth held a few inches away.
And a voice says her name.
“Sabine. Breathe.”
She lies there in his arms with her eyes shut for two seconds longer than the drill requires.
What she is checking for — and she knows exactly what she is checking for, she has known since she got in the water — is fear.

She has not been carried in this water since the fourth of April nine years ago, when a man walking a dog on the western path got her out because she could not get herself out, and she cannot remember any of it, and she has spent nine years being certain that if she were ever held in this water again it would come back and take her apart.
There is no fear.

She lies limp in four degrees of water at the eastern end of the Cut with her eyes closed and a stranger’s hand under her jaw and the whole black column of it underneath her, ninety-four metres straight down, and what she feels is not fear and it is not relief and it is not even the ordinary animal comfort of being held.
It is recognition.
It is the feeling of arriving at a house you used to live in and finding your own coat still on the hook.
She opens her eyes.
“You did it right,” she says. “All four. Good.”
“You went completely,” Aurel says. He sounds slightly shaken. “I’ve never — you were properly gone. I couldn’t tell.”
“That’s the point of the drill.”
“No, I mean I couldn’t tell whether you’d gone on purpose.”
Sabine treads water and looks at him.
“Neither could I,” she says.
SEVEN. 20 METRES
The punches start at about a minute and a half and they are the reason most people never get past two.

Sabine teaches them on land, in a chair, because that is the only way to teach them honestly. She sits a beginner down, has them breathe normally, and then has them hold, and she says nothing at all for the first minute, and then when the first one lands she says: there.

The diaphragm is a sheet of muscle under the lungs and it is not on anybody’s side. It has one job, which is to pull down and let air in, and it has been doing that job about twenty thousand times a day since before you were born without ever once being asked. When the waste starts building, the alarm goes to the diaphragm and the diaphragm tries to do its job.
You have your throat shut. So it pulls against nothing.

The result is a hit. From inside, under the ribs, hard enough to move a body in water. And then a pause, and then another, and the gaps get shorter and the hits get stronger, and there are people who have been diving for twenty years who will tell you honestly that the worst three minutes of their lives are the ones they chose.
The name divers use is contractions, which is a mealy word for it. Sabine has always called them the punches. She has never had a beginner fail to understand her.

“Here’s the whole of it,” she tells them, always, on the land, in the chair. “The punches are not the problem. The punches are not a warning. They mean the rubbish has reached a level, and the level is nowhere near the level that matters. You have — depending on who you are — between forty per cent and sixty per cent of your dive left when the first one lands. Sixty per cent. You are barely halfway.

“So you will be hit, repeatedly, by your own body, and it will feel exactly like drowning, and the correct response is to do absolutely nothing about it. Not to fight it. Not to brace. Not to breathe. To let it happen and let the next one happen and keep going. That’s the sport. That’s all of it. Everything else is fins.”
Aurel passes through them on his second Sunday and the way he does it is what starts the thing in her chest that will not sit down again.

She is at ten metres with her face out, one arm through the buoy strap, watching him come up from thirty-five. Thirty-five is the number she has given him and he has taken the number without argument, which she noted, because divers who take a number without argument are usually storing up an argument for later.

She sees him at fifteen. He is not swimming. He is coming up with his arms at his sides and his legs going in a slow economical beat that she would not change a thing about, and even at fifteen metres in bad light she can see him get hit, because the whole shape of him jolts and then resumes.
Then again. Then again, closer together.
And he does not alter.

That is the thing. She has coached eighty-odd people in this hole and every single one of them alters. They speed up, or they clench, or their kick loses its rhythm and turns into a scramble, or they lift their chin, which is the worst and the most human, as if the surface could be reached by wanting. Every diver alters, and a coach’s job for the first three years is to teach them to alter less.

Aurel is hit six times in the last twelve metres and his kick does not change by a beat. He arrives at the surface on exactly the rhythm he left the bottom with, and he takes three breaths, small then larger then larger, and takes the mask off, and finds her eyes, and holds up the circle.
“I’m okay.”
Sabine hears herself say, “Time,” and her own voice sounds distant.
“Two forty-one.”
“Depth?”
“Thirty-five.”
“Punches?”
“Started about ninety seconds.” He is treading, easy, and there is water in his eyebrows and he is not shivering yet. “Yes. Six or seven. Is that early?”
“It’s normal.” She makes herself say the next thing in the tone she would use with anybody. “You didn’t change.”
“I wasn’t supposed to change.”
“No. You weren’t.” She unhooks her arm from the strap. “Most people can’t manage that in their first five years.”

He shrugs, and this time the shrug is loose because he is not cold enough yet to be locked, and he says, in perfect innocence, the sentence that she will still be turning over at two in the morning three weeks from now:
“They don’t feel like mine.”
She takes it apart afterwards, driving home, and she can make it innocent four different ways.

He might mean what a hundred divers mean, which is that the punches are involuntary and so are experienced as something happening to you, not something you are doing. That is true and unremarkable and there is a whole literature of people saying it in slightly different words.

He might mean the ordinary dissociation that comes to anybody in a cold dark hole with a shut throat. The mind steps back a pace. Everybody’s does. It is how the sport is possible at all: the diver watches the body from the next seat along and takes an interest.
He might mean nothing. People say things.

She gets home and puts the light on and stands in the kitchen with her coat still on, and she makes herself say the fourth version out loud, because there is nobody in the house and because if she does not say it in a kitchen she will end up saying it in a worse place.
“They don’t feel like mine,” she says. “Because there are two sets.”
The house does not respond. The house is a two-bedroom terrace with slate on the roof out of the hole she will not go into and a boiler that comes on at six.

She had been thirty-five. It had been the fourth of April and the water had been four degrees, and by the second week of that March she and Elvire had been at seventy metres on a line that Elvire had rigged with her own hands, and Sabine had told her, on the drive back from a session in the second week of March, in a car with the heater on, with a bag of chips between them on the handbrake, they don’t feel like mine any more.
And Elvire had said: Whose, then?
And Sabine had laughed, because it had been funny.
She does not sleep. At four she gives it up and comes downstairs and gets out the box.

The box lives at the back of the cupboard under the stairs and contains: two logbooks in Elvire’s hand and one in her own; a folded and refolded newspaper page; a coroner’s summary with a stamp on the front and four paragraphs on the inside; a photograph of two women on a slate ledge at the western end of the Cut, both laughing, both in wetsuits peeled to the waist, one of them holding up a thermos as though it were a trophy; and a mask.
She takes the mask out. It is nine years old and the skirt has gone hard and yellow, and the strap is a wide black strap, the good kind, the kind you had to send away for then.
She sits on the floor of the hall with it in her lap for a long time.

Then she puts it back, and puts the lid on the box, and pushes the box to the back of the cupboard, and at half past five she puts her coat on over her nightclothes and drives out to the Cut in the dark and stands at the top of the ramp until it is light enough to see the buoy.
She does not go down to the water. It is important to her, in a way she could not defend to anybody, that on that particular morning she does not go down the ramp and put her hand in.
“You’re doing forty on Sunday,” she tells Aurel on the Thursday.
“You said thirty-five.”
“I’ve changed it.”
He looks at her, and there is a fractional thing in his face, and it is not what she expected. It is not eagerness.
“Why,” he says.
“Because you’re ready for forty and you’d have got there on your own by August, and if you’re going to get there I would rather you got there with me hanging at fifteen holding a watch.”
“That’s not why.”
Sabine, who has been managing people in and out of dangerous water since she was twenty-two, is briefly and completely stopped.
“No,” she says. “It’s a third of it.”
“That’s the second time you’ve given me a third of something.”
“You’ll get the rest eventually.”
“Will I?”
“No,” she says, and it is the most honest sentence she says to him in the whole of April.
He laughs. She does not.

Forty metres is where the air starts behaving like a drug. She knows that and he knows that, because he reads, and he has probably read a better account of it than the one she would give him. He has not asked her about it. In fourteen months of teaching himself out of books he has not, as far as she can tell, once asked anybody anything.

She has decided to send a twenty-six-year-old man past the depth where the water starts talking, and to be on the surface with a watch when it happens, and she has told herself four separate true reasons why, and the true reasons form a wall she cannot see over.

Behind the wall is the thing she said to Elvire in a car in March with a bag of chips on the handbrake. Behind the wall is the fourth of April. Behind the wall is a mask with a wide black strap in a box under the stairs, and a question she has not been able to put down in nine years, which is not what happened to Elvire.
It is: would anybody else have said no?
EIGHT. 20 METRES
