Divers alternated. One dives, one holds the surface. Four dives completed between 09:40 and 11:15, depths of thirty, forty-five, fifty-five and sixty metres, all logged in the deceased’s own hand in a book recovered from her car.
At 11:31 the deceased entered the water for a fifth dive with an intended depth of seventy-two metres. S. Vasseur held the surface.
At approximately 11:34 S. Vasseur descended to an unrecorded depth, described by her in the statement as “as far as I could get.”

At 11:41 S. Vasseur surfaced alone. She was assisted from the water by a man walking a dog on the western path who had heard her shouting. She was not able to tell him what had happened for some minutes. Emergency services attended at 12:04.
The body was recovered on 9 April by a police dive team using equipment and gas.
Depth of recovery: sixty-eight metres. Four metres above the plate.
Cause of death: drowning, consequent on loss of consciousness due to lack of oxygen.
ITEM 2. Why this file is still open.
It is open because I never closed it and because nobody has ever asked me to.

The company settled in eleven weeks. There was no claim to fight: the deceased had no dependants, the site had no formal operator at the time, and the family in Charleroi wanted the body and the logbook and nothing else. My employer’s exposure was assessed at nil. My recommendation was a formal notice to the council regarding unsupervised access, which was made and which produced, eventually, a locked gate that anybody can climb and a sign-in book that anybody can not sign.
The professional matter was concluded in eleven weeks.

I am going to write the rest of this down as though somebody else will read it, because that is the only discipline I have found that keeps it honest, and because on the days when I am least honest I am aware that I am building a case rather than keeping a record.
ITEM 3. The statement.
I have the statement. I have read it perhaps two hundred times over nine years, which I recognise is not a normal number.

It is four hundred words long. It was taken at Ossay police station on the evening of 4 April by an officer who had never taken a statement about diving and who wrote down, faithfully, everything he was told, including the parts that make no sense, which is the only reason this file has ever been of any use to me.
The four hundred words are, in summary:

She went down at 11:31. I held the surface. At about three minutes I went down after her. I got as far as I could get. I could not see her. I came up. I do not know how long I was down. I do not know how deep I went. I came up and there was nobody there.

That is the substance and it is unimpeachable. Every diver I have ever spoken to about it, and I have spoken to eleven, has said the same thing: that is exactly what would have happened, and there is nothing in it to question, and she is lucky to be alive, and going down after a diver who has been under three minutes at that depth is the single most dangerous thing a human being can voluntarily do, and she did it, and she should not have, and everybody would have.
But.
In the statement there are two sentences that are not in the summary, and they are the two sentences the officer wrote down because he did not know they were unusual.
The first is: “I got as far as I could get and then I could not make myself go further.”
The second is: “There was somebody there and it was not her.”

The officer asked, according to his own note in the margin, whether she meant another diver had been present at the site. She said no. He asked whether she meant a member of the public. She said no. He wrote: witness distressed, possibly confused, cold exposure. Did not pursue.
ITEM 4. What I have done with those two sentences over nine years.

I have shown them to a doctor, who explained to me at length and with great patience the state a body is in after a rapid deep descent on no air, and used a word I have since read a great deal about, and said, in effect: of course she said that. They say all sorts. It isn’t evidence of anything except that she nearly died.

I have shown them to a diving coach in Brest who charged me nothing and told me that people see things down there so routinely that the coaching community has stopped remarking on it. He said the divers he worries about are not the ones who see things. They are the ones who go back looking.

I have looked, twice, into whether a third person was at the Cut on the morning of 4 April, and both times found nothing, because the answer to that question is a sign-in book which for that year was a spiral notebook kept in an unlocked hut.
And I have asked my sister once, nine years ago, in a hospital corridor, what she meant.
She said: “Nothing. I was gone.”
She has never said another word about it, to me or to anyone, and in nine years she has not put her face in that water, and until this month I believed those two facts were one fact.
ITEM 5. What is new.
Three items.

(a) My employer has engaged S. Vasseur to produce a water safety assessment on the Cut, in support of a premium review the lease-holder has been pursuing for two years. The engagement was made on my recommendation.
I want that sentence to sit on the page on its own for a moment.

I recommended her. I was asked in February for the name of somebody whose finding on that water would not be argued with, and I gave them my sister’s, and I did it in four seconds without appearing to think about it, and I have had five months to work out why.

Her name will be believed because of the fourth of April. That is the only reason it is worth anything to an insurer, and I knew that when I gave it, and so the commercial value of my sister’s reputation derives entirely from the death of Elvire Baudry, and I am the person who put a price on it.
(b) K. Nizan, 26, of the Ossay road, has signed into the Cut ninety-one times in fourteen months, unaccompanied on eighty-eight of those occasions, and by his own admission to me on

16 April has reached thirty-one metres alone. I flagged this in March, to a lease-holder twenty miles away who has never set foot on the site. He did nothing. I did nothing further, and I want that recorded too, because it was a choice, and the reason for it was that a barred diver drives to a reservoir.

(c) On 16 April I found my sister in the hut at the Cut with this young man, a heater on, two cups of tea, and a diagram drawn on a page torn out of the sign-in book. She has since taken him on as a diver and is holding the surface for him. She has been in the water, in a suit, above him, three times.

I have been waiting nine years for her to go near that water again, and I find that now it has happened I am not relieved, and that the shape of what I feel is closer to the shape of what I felt at 12:04 on the fourth of April, standing in the gravel, before anybody had told me anything.
ITEM 6. My own position, stated for the record.

A finding of satisfactorily managed on this site is worth eleven thousand a year to the lease-holder and rather less than nothing to me, and the person who will decide whether that finding stands is me.

That is the position. I recommended the author. I will assess the document. There is a form for declaring an interest and I have had it in a drawer since February and I have not filled it in, and I have told myself four separate true things about why, and I am going to write the untrue thing down instead, for the reason I gave at Item 2.

If I declare the interest, the work goes to a colleague in Rennes who has never seen this water, and he reads eleven pages and signs them, and it is over in a fortnight, and I never find out anything.
If I keep it, I get to read every word my sister writes about the fourth of April, under her own signature, in a document she knows I will be assessing.
I have wanted for nine years to be told. I have arranged, at some cost and with some skill, to be told in writing by a woman who will not say it out loud.

I want to be precise about my own condition here, because a file that is only honest about other people is worthless. There are two things I want, and they are not compatible, and I have been carrying both of them for nine years without ever putting them in the same sentence:
I want to know what my sister meant.
And I want her to have been at fault.
If I am given the second I will stop looking for the first. I am aware of that. I have been aware of it for some time.

Attend Sunday. Observe. Do not intervene.
Obtain, if it can be obtained without asking, whatever Nizan is writing in that notebook.
NINE. 30 METRES
The Sunday is the best day of the year so far, which is the sort of detail Sabine will resent later.

No wind. The surface of the Cut goes glass and holds the shape of the walls upside down in it, and you can see the line for the first four metres instead of the first two, and the water has come up a degree and a half since March, which is nothing and which everybody notices.
Maude comes and stands at the top of the ramp with her laptop bag and her glasses and does not come down, and Sabine lets her stand there.

They rig to forty-five and Sabine puts the plate at forty, and she checks the rig herself twice, and then a third time, and she is aware that she is doing the thing where competence is used as a place to hide.
“Two dives,” she tells Aurel. “Thirty-two to warm, then forty. I’m at fifteen with a lanyard on. If I put my arm out flat, that’s up, and you don’t get to have an opinion.”
“Understood.”
“Say the arithmetic.”

He says it. Time down, time at the plate, time up, plus the third she adds on top of everybody’s numbers as a matter of policy. He has it exactly. He has had it exactly every time she has asked, for a month.
“Good,” she says. “Last thing. At forty the air in you starts working like a drug. You’ve read about it.”
“I’ve read about it.”

“Reading about it is nothing. Here’s what it actually is: at that depth the stuff you’re carrying in your chest starts behaving the way a couple of drinks behave, except you can’t tell that it’s happened, because the thing that would tell you is the thing that’s affected. And it doesn’t feel like being drunk. It feels like being extremely clear. It feels like finally being clear. People get down there and become very interested in something and forget entirely what they came for.”
“What sort of thing.”
“Anything. A stone. Their own hand.” Sabine adjusts her strap. “It also does the other thing, and this is the one I want you to hear. It makes people certain that somebody is with them.”
Aurel’s face does not change.

“That’s very common,” she says. “It’s so common it’s boring. It happens to climbers at altitude and to men in lifeboats and to people who walk across ice for weeks. There’s a whole literature. It’s the oldest trick the head has: you take away the light and the sound and the up and the down, and you leave a brain with nothing to work on, and a brain with nothing to work on will make you a companion out of whatever’s lying about. It’s the same machinery that makes you see a face in a curtain. It just has more room.”
“All right.”
“So if it happens, it means you’re low and cold and deep. That’s all it means. It’s a reading on a gauge.” She looks at him. “Do you understand what I’m telling you?”
And Aurel Nizan says, “Yes,” and means, she is entirely certain, something other than what she said.
The warm dive is unremarkable.

He goes to thirty-two and comes back in two minutes flat and does the rite correctly and sits on the surface for six minutes, and Sabine notes his colour and his shivering and the way his hands move, and everything is where it should be, and there is nobody to give her a nod that means he’s good, stop worrying, which she notices, and which she has arranged.
Then he does the breathe-up for forty and he does it beautifully, and at 13:22 he folds at the waist and goes.
She watches the line.

That is all there is to do. From fifteen metres with her face out, there is one rope and there is the amount of tension in the rope, and there is a watch on her wrist, and there is a silence that people who have never done it imagine to be peaceful.

Forty metres. Down in fifty seconds if he does it right. Six seconds at the plate. Fifty-five up, sixty with the punches. Two minutes six, and she has told him two twenty, and she will start being unhappy at two forty and she will go at three.
At two twenty the line has not moved.
At two thirty she looks at the buoy, and at the watch, and at the buoy.
At two forty Sabine puts her face in the water and looks down.
There is nothing to see. There has never been anything to see. Twelve metres of grey and then the edge and then the thing past the edge, and the line running away into it with no diver on it.
At two fifty she takes a breath and drops.

She is fifteen metres down before she understands what she is doing, and the understanding arrives with the cold on her face, which throws the switch it has been waiting nine years to throw, and her heart goes out from under her like a floor giving way, and she keeps going.
Twenty metres. Twenty-five.

The colour is gone out of everything and she has not been here in nine years and her body knows the exact texture of this depth the way a hand knows a bannister in the dark. Twenty-eight. Thirty. Her ears are behind and she clears them badly and something in the left one gives a small dry crack.
And she stops.

She does not decide to stop. She stops the way she stopped nine years ago at a depth she has never been able to name, and the sentence arrives in her whole and finished and in the officer’s handwriting: I got as far as I could get and then I could not make myself go further.
Below her the line goes down into it.
There is nothing on the line.
She comes up.

She comes up badly, kicking, too fast, and she breaks the surface with her mouth already open and hauls at the air in exactly the way she has told eight hundred people never to do, and for four or five seconds the sky goes grainy at the edges and she has to hold the buoy strap with both hands.
Then she gets her eyes clear of the water and turns her head, and he is up.
He is up.

He is twenty metres away, on the other side of the buoy, treading, with his mask in his hand and his hair flat and his lips the colour lips go. He has been up, she works out later, for perhaps thirty seconds. He came up quietly, and she did not see him do it, because she was looking down.
Sabine gets to him with three strokes and a hand on his shoulder that is not a coaching hand.
“Time,” she says. “Say your time.”
“I don’t know.”
“Say your depth.”
“Forty.” He looks at her. “I went to forty. I put my hand on the plate. I turned. I came up.”
“You were under four minutes and eleven seconds.”
“That’s not right.”
“I have it on the watch.”
“That’s not right,” he says again, and there is not one particle of argument in it. He says it the way a man reads out a number that has come up wrong on a bill.

She takes hold of his chin, which she has no right to do, and turns his face into the light and looks at his eyes, and his eyes are steady. She takes his wrist. His pulse is where it should be, coming back up out of the twenties in the ordinary way. He is shivering appropriately. He is not confused. He knows the date, he knows her name, he knows what he had for breakfast, he knows the arithmetic.
Four minutes and eleven seconds.

She does the sums that afternoon on the back of a page from the sign-in book and then again that night in a chair at home and then again on the Monday, and the sums are not close. Four eleven at forty metres in four-degree water is not a hard dive for a man of his ability; it is a dive from a different sport. His best hold on the surface, lying still and warm and doing nothing at all, is five twenty. To spend four eleven working in cold black water at forty metres and come up with steady eyes and a good pulse and no shakes is not an achievement. It is a wrong answer.
There are three explanations and she works through all of them properly, because she is a coach and that is what a coach does.
One: her watch is wrong. She checks the watch against the clock in the hut and against the phone in her coat and against the speaking clock. The watch is right.

Two: he is lying about the depth — he did not go to forty, he went to twenty and hung there. She was at fifteen with her face out and she felt him go past her in the water, which is a thing you feel rather than see, and she has been feeling divers go past her for twenty-two years, and he went past her going down and he did not come back up through her.

Three: he is doing something to the timetable. Which is the only explanation left, and it is the one every coach reaches for, because divers cheat their own tables constantly and always in the same direction, and there are four or five ways to do it and every single one of them is a form of stealing from an account you cannot see the balance of.
She spends four days convinced it is the third thing.

She has a whole speech prepared. She has, God help her, been looking forward to giving it, because a diver who cheats the tables is a problem she has solved thirty times, and a solved problem is a comfort.

On the Sunday, before she can give the speech, Aurel comes up out of the water from thirty metres, and takes three breaths, and takes the mask all the way off his face rather than pushing it up, and finds her eyes and holds them for a full three seconds, and lifts his hand and makes the circle.
“I’m okay,” he says.
And then, treading easily, in the tone of a man asking whether there is any more tea:
“When can we do sixty?”
Sabine, holding the buoy strap, hears herself say: “Why sixty.”
“Because forty wasn’t far enough.”
“Far enough for what?”

And Aurel Nizan thinks about it. That is the part she will keep. He does not answer quickly and he does not answer defensively. He floats there in a hole in the moor with four hundred thousand tonnes of black water under him and he genuinely considers the question, as though it has occurred to him that he might not have the answer either.
“To get to where it starts,” he says.
II. THE FALL
TEN. 30 METRES
From the log of Aurel Nizan. Fifth notebook. The hand is smaller than in the fourth and much more even.
Nobody told me about the falling.

That is not a complaint about the books. The books mention it. There is a paragraph in every one of them, and the paragraph says that past a certain depth your body stops floating and starts sinking, and that you can therefore stop swimming, and that this is called the free fall, and that divers enjoy it.
Divers enjoy it.
I have read that sentence perhaps forty times and I did not understand for fifteen months that I was reading a man standing in front of a door describing the door.

Here is the arithmetic of it, because the arithmetic is the honest part. A body with air in its chest floats. That is why you can lie on the surface without effort. As you go down the water squeezes the air in you smaller, and the smaller it gets the less it lifts you, and somewhere between twenty-five and thirty-five metres — it depends on your build and how much you took down — the sums cross over. Above that line you are a cork and the water is pushing you home. Below it you are a stone.

There is no announcement. That is what nobody writes down. You are working, kicking, spending, and you have been spending since the surface, and then at some point in the middle of a kick the kick is not doing anything, because the kick is not needed, and you put your legs together and your arms flat at your sides and you stop.
And you keep going down.

Sabine calls it the fall and she calls it the best thing in the sport and she is wrong about what it is, and I do not think she is wrong by accident. I have started to think she is wrong on purpose, the way you say a thing slightly wrong in order not to say it right in front of somebody.
What she says is: the water stops fighting you.

That is not it. Fighting is the wrong frame entirely, because fighting has two parties in it and up to that moment there is only one. Above thirty metres the water is not fighting anybody. The water is not doing anything at all. It is a quantity, it has properties, and if you go into it hard it will hold you up because of what it is, in the way that a floor holds you up. Nobody says the floor is fighting them.
What happens at thirty metres is not that the water stops resisting.
It is that the water starts participating.

I have tried five ways to write this and they are all worse than the plain version, so here is the plain version. Up to thirty metres I am doing something to the water. Past thirty metres the water is doing something to me. And the something is not a push. It has no force in it. It is closer to consent — as though up to that point I have been an object being tolerated and past that point I have been agreed to.
The other thing about the fall is the speed, and the speed is the part that made me stop diving for eleven days in March and think about whether I was going to keep doing this.

You accelerate. Obviously you accelerate; you are a stone. But you have nothing to accelerate against. There is no wind, no ground going by, no sound of movement, no horizon, no reference of any kind. The line is there — I use the line now, Sabine has beaten that into me — and the line is going past my hand, and that is the only fact in the world that says you are moving.
So take the hand off the line.

I did it on the fourth of April, which I did not know at the time was a date that means anything, and I did it at thirty-eight metres in the dark, and for eleven or twelve seconds I fell through a place with no up, no down, no sound, no colour, no reference and no evidence that I was moving.
And it was not falling. It cannot have been falling, because falling is a relation between a thing and a place it is going, and there was no place.
It was being taken in. Down is the wrong word, and in is a better word, and the best word is a word I am not going to write in a notebook.
I got the hand back on the line and I came up and I sat in the car for a long time.
I have got to sixty.
That is the plain report and I will do the plain report first before the rest of it, because Sabine says a log with the feelings at the top is a log written for somebody else.

Sixty metres, four dives across two Sundays, plate at sixty, line to sixty-eight. Fall begins at thirty-one on the first dive and twenty-nine on the fourth, which means my chest is closing earlier, which means the training is working. Time on the last one: three fifty-one. Turn at sixty, no hang. Punches from a minute forty. Six on the way down and I lost count on the way up. Cold in the left ear on all four. Sabine at fifteen with the watch.
Correct on the surface all four times. Three breaths, mask off, eyes, circle, I’m okay.
Now the rest of it.

Sabine sat me down in the hut before the first sixty and told me about the drug. She did it well. She said that at forty the stuff in my chest starts working like a couple of drinks, and that I would not be able to tell, because the thing that would tell me is the thing affected. She said it does not feel like being drunk. She said it feels like being clear. She said: it feels like finally being clear.
I have thought about the word finally quite a lot since. She did not have to put that word in.
Then she told me about the companion.

She said it happens to everybody. She said it happens to climbers on mountains and men in lifeboats and people who walk across ice, and that there is a whole literature, and that it is the oldest trick the head has — take away the light and the sound and the up and the down, leave the brain with nothing to work on, and a brain with nothing to work on will build you a companion out of whatever is lying about. She said it is the same machinery that makes a face in a curtain. She said it has more room.
She said: if it happens, it means you’re low and cold and deep. That’s all it means. It’s a reading on a gauge.
I said yes.
Here is what I want to put in the notebook, and then I am going to stop for tonight.

Everything she told me is true. I have checked it since, I have read the papers she was summarising, and she was summarising them accurately and generously and without inventing anything. A man in my position, low and cold and deep in a hole with no light in it, will be given company by his own head, and the company will feel entirely real, and that this has been established for a hundred years by people better qualified than me.
But she told me before it happened.

I want that on the page. She sat me in a hut with a heater on and told me, unprompted, in detail, before my first dive past forty, exactly what I was going to meet and exactly how to dismiss it. She has known me six weeks. She has not been in that water in nine years, and she got a suit out for me, and she has never once said why, and she has twice now told me she was giving me a third of a reason.
You do not warn a man that carefully about a face in a curtain.
You warn a man that carefully when you are hoping he will come up and tell you that he saw one.

I am not going to write what happened at sixty yet. Not because I am being coy in a notebook that nobody reads. Because I have noticed that when I write a thing down I finish with it, and I am not finished.
Two facts only, then, and both of them are facts and not feelings.

The first is that the punches, past forty, arrive in pairs. One and then, about a beat later, another, slightly stronger. This is not in any of the books. I have looked. There is a great deal about the punches being irregular, which they are, and nothing about them being doubled. I have counted. On the last dive it was six pairs down and I lost count up, and it was pairs all the way.
The second is that the second one of each pair does not feel like mine.

I said that to Sabine, on the surface, in April, about the ordinary punches at thirty-five, and she went very still and asked me nothing. I have thought about her face a lot. At the time I thought I had said something stupid.
I am beginning to think I said something she has been waiting nine years to hear somebody say.
ELEVEN. 40 METRES
The arithmetic does not work and Sabine spends the last week of May proving it.

She does it properly. She has kept tables on eighty-one divers over twenty-two years and she knows what a good progression looks like on paper: a curve that climbs and then flattens, with a scatter of bad days in it, and the bad days are the point — the bad days are how you know you are looking at a human being and not at somebody’s hopes.
Aurel’s page has no bad days on it.

She lays it out on the kitchen table on the Tuesday with the good lamp on. Fourteen months of his own logs, which he hands over without hesitation the moment she asks, in four notebooks, and then her own six weeks on top.

Depth, ascending, with no plateau: thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-five, forty, forty-eight, fifty-five, sixty. Time under, ascending. Surface interval, descending — he needs less rest between dives now than he did in March, which is backwards, that is not a thing that improves, the debt is supposed to accumulate across a session and it accumulates for everybody.
She goes through it three times looking for the theft.

There are four common ways a diver steals from his own tables and she knows all four in her hands. There is the extra air taken at the surface, packed in past what the chest wants, which buys thirty seconds and costs you a lung eventually. There is the shallow lie — the number in the book that never happened. There is the hidden line-pull, hauling yourself down hand over hand while claiming to have swum it. And there is the one nobody talks about, which is coming up on the very last of it every single time and calling that a normal dive, so that the whole table is written in a currency of near-misses.
Not one of them fits.

She has watched him pack and he does not pack. His hands never leave his sides in the fall — she has been at fifteen watching him come up out of it four Sundays running and she would see it. And a man who is coming up on the last of it every time gets the shakes, sooner or later, and gets them in front of somebody, and Aurel Nizan has not shaken once in fifteen months and ninety-nine dives.
That is the number that stops her, in the end. Ninety-nine dives, nineteen of them past forty metres, and not one episode. Not a wobble in the jaw. Not a bad surfacing.

Roughly one competition dive in ten ends with somebody shaking on the surface. That is the published figure and it has not moved in twenty years and it applies to the best divers in the world under judges with medics on the platform. It is so ordinary that nobody remarks on it. Sabine has had the shakes four times in her life. Elvire had them eleven times and kept a tally in the back of a book with a small tick for each, because Elvire found them funny.
Nineteen dives past forty metres in cold water with no line-pull and no packing and no rest and no bad days and no shakes.
She sits back in the chair.

The correct professional conclusion is available and she can see it from where she is sitting: this man is an outlier, some people are, write it up and be glad. Every coach in the world would take it. There is one in every generation who arrives already built, and the sport keeps a small mythology of them, and the mythology exists precisely so that coaches have somewhere to put the arithmetic when it stops working.
Sabine puts the pencil down and says, to an empty kitchen, “No.”
She goes at it from the other end on the Wednesday, which means she goes at the depth.

Forty metres is where the air turns. She has explained this to perhaps three hundred people and she has a form of words she trusts, and the form of words is a lie of scale — accurate in every particular, and pitched to make the thing sound like weather rather than what it is.
What she tells people: at forty metres the stuff you are carrying starts working like a couple of drinks.

What is actually happening is that the pressure has squeezed her diver’s chest to a fifth of what it was on the surface, and everything in it is now dissolved into him at a concentration his body has never met before, and one of the things in it is a gas that is inert at the surface and is a sedative at depth. Not a stimulant. Not a hallucinogen, whatever divers like to say in bars. A sedative, of the same broad family as the things they give you before a small operation.

And what a sedative does — the actual mechanism, the part she has read four papers on and never once said out loud to a beginner — is that it interferes with the traffic. It does not add anything. It does not put a voice in your head. It slows the passing of information between the parts of a brain, so that the parts stop cross-checking each other, and one of the things a brain does with all that cross-checking, constantly, tirelessly, unnoticed, is decide which of the many things going on inside it are me and which are not me.
That decision is not a fact. It is a running calculation. It is performed several times a second, for free, for your entire life, and you have never once been aware of it.
At forty metres you begin to buy it on credit. At sixty you are behind on the payments.

So a man at sixty metres in the dark has a brain that is still generating everything a brain generates — impulses, images, intentions, the small constant hum of a body reporting in — and has lost the machinery that stamps each one mine.

And unstamped material has to go somewhere. It does not stop existing. It gets attributed. The head is very old and very practical and it has one enormous well-worn category for anything that is happening and is not you, and that category is: someone else is here.
Sabine writes this out longhand on the Wednesday night, four pages, in the clean flat prose she uses for reports, and reads it back, and it is completely satisfactory.
It explains the pairs.

That is the thing she is most pleased about for about ninety minutes. The doubled punches he described to her — one his, one a beat later that does not feel like his — are not two events. They are one irregular event, arriving in a body whose attribution machinery is failing, and half of it is coming through unstamped. There is nothing there. There is one diaphragm doing one thing badly and a brain that has run out of the ability to sign for it.

She reads the four pages again at midnight and finds that she has written a flawless account of how a man alone in the dark manufactures a companion, and that not one line of it is any use at all, because she is not trying to work out whether the companion is real.
She has never wondered that. Not for nine years. Not for one hour.
What she wants to know is why it takes him four minutes and eleven seconds to do a dive that should take two.
Thursday she teaches the beginners and does it well, on the shelf, in three metres, and is present for none of it.
Afterwards she coils line on her own in the last of the light, which is a job that leaves the hands busy and the rest of a person entirely free, and which is why she has always hated it.

In April she was watching his kick. Now she is doing sums, and the sums are a place to stand, and she has been standing in them for three weeks so as not to have to look at the thing she has actually observed nineteen times from fifteen metres with her face in the water.

He goes past her on the way down like a man getting into bed. Not calm — calm is an achievement, calm is something a diver does. Relaxed, which is something that happens to a diver when the water agrees with him.
And he comes back up past her more relaxed than he went down.

She gets to the end of the line and ties it off and stands in the dark at the top of the ramp with the coil over her forearm and says it out loud, once, to nobody, in the flat voice she uses for the bleak version.
“He’s better on the way up than the way down.”

Which cannot be. Because the way up is the expensive half. The way up is where the account empties and the pressure comes off and the lights go out without warning, and there is no diver in the world, at any level, in any water, who is more comfortable at the end of a dive than at the start of it. The whole shape of the sport is a curve going down. That is not a rule, it is not a convention, it is not something a talented man can be an exception to. It is the bill arriving.

The question she cannot put to anybody, and which she therefore puts to a coil of line on her own forearm in the dark at the top of a ramp, is whether on Sunday, when he comes past her on the way up, he will look like a man coming back.

There is nobody to ask. She has arranged that. She could have had four people on this water on a Sunday — there is a club forty miles off that would send them and be glad — and she has kept it to herself and one boy and a watch, and she has had four separate good reasons for that all summer, and she is standing in the cold holding a rope and she cannot get any of the four to look at her.

“Sixty on Sunday,” she says. “Then seventy the Sunday after.” She picks up the crate. “He’s asked for ninety-four. He’ll get to ninety-four by August whatever I put on the plate, and he’ll get there with me at fifteen holding a watch or he’ll get there on a Tuesday afternoon with nobody in the department who knows he’s in the water.”
Those are not, she is aware, the only two things she could do.
She carries the crate up the ramp.
TWELVE. 50 METRES
From the log of Aurel Nizan. Fifth notebook, continued.
I am going to try to write the dark properly and I expect to fail.

Everybody who has been down there says it is like nothing else and then reaches for something else to compare it to, and the something else is always a room with the light off, and a room with the light off is not it. In a room the dark is a condition of the room. Take the light away and the dark is what is left over — it is the absence, it is what remains when you subtract.
Fifty metres in the Cut is not an absence. It is the most present thing I have ever been inside.

It has temperature. It has weight. It comes in layers, and the layers have edges, and I will come to that. It arrives the way a substance arrives: you go into it, it is displaced around you, it closes again behind. If somebody told me tomorrow that the black at fifty metres was a material with a name and a price per tonne I would not be surprised. It behaves like one.

The nearest honest comparison I have found is not visual at all. It is the feeling of a wool blanket over your head as a child, in summer, in the afternoon, when you have made a tent of the bed and you are not hiding from anybody and you have been in there for an hour and the air has gone warm and used. That is the company of it. That is the weight and the closeness and the sense that you are inside something rather than in the middle of nothing.
Except the Cut is four degrees.
The colour dies on a timetable and I have written the timetable out before, so I will only put down what surprised me, which is that the timetable does not end.
You would think it ends. You would think there is a point where all the colour has gone and after that it is simply black and stays black, and there is nothing further to report.

But it keeps going. Past thirty-five, when the last of the green has gone and there is technically no colour left, the not-colour continues to change. There are perhaps four distinct not-colours between thirty-five and sixty and I could recognise any of them blind, and I have no words at all for the differences between them and no confidence that they exist outside my own head. It is like being asked to distinguish four kinds of silence. You can. You cannot say how.
The one at fifty is the one I have written about before as the closed eye. I stand by that. It has a grain in it. The grain moves.

I have read enough now to know what the grain is. My eyes are not receiving anything down there — there is nothing to receive — and an eye that is receiving nothing does not go quiet, it goes on generating, and what it generates is noise. Static, essentially, from the machinery itself. The interesting part is that it is the only thing down there my own body is still making for me on the outside.
Every other sense has been taken away or turned inward. That grain is the last manufactured thing.
So it is not true that there is nothing to see at fifty metres.
There is exactly one thing to see and it is your own eyes running with nothing in them.
The sound goes before the colour is finished and it goes in a way I did not expect.
I had assumed silence. Everybody assumes silence. Water is quiet, and deep water must be quieter, and the deepest must be silent.
It is the opposite. The sound does not go away, it collapses inward, and what is left is enormous.

By about twenty metres the outside is gone: no birds, no wind on the surface, no gravel under anybody’s boots on the platform, no voices, nothing. And in the space where all of that was there is now one sound and it is my own heart, and I want to be careful about how I put this, because the obvious way to put it is that it gets louder.

It does not get louder. It gets bigger. It has size. It has a room to be in and the room is the whole of the water. And it is slow — that is the part nobody prepares you for — because the switch has taken it down into the twenties and there are nearly four seconds between one and the next, and in those four seconds there is no sound in the universe at all.
Four seconds is a long time. Try it now, with a watch. Four seconds of complete silence, and then something the size of the sky, and then four seconds again.
That is what fifty metres is. That is the metronome the rest of it happens on.
The layers.

This is the part that I have not been able to explain to Sabine, and I have tried twice, and both times she has given me the correct information and both times the correct information has been beside the point.

The Cut is not one temperature. It is stacked. There are bands of water at different temperatures sitting on top of one another, and they do not mix, and going down you pass through them one after another, and the boundaries between them are thin.

Sabine says: sheets of cold. She says it happens in every deep still water in the world, and it is a matter of density, and the sheets sit where they sit for months, and in the Cut there are three or four of them and the sharpest is somewhere between forty-two and forty-five metres and has been there since February.
All correct. I have read it. Here is what she has not got and I do not think it is her fault.
A sheet of cold, described that way, is a thing you pass through. You are here, then you are colder, and the change happens across half a metre.

That is not the sensation. The sensation is not of passing through. It is of something being drawn aside — the way a curtain is drawn aside, or a net, or one of those thin gauze things people used to hang over a bed in summer. There is a moment of contact across the whole face and body at once, and a moment of resistance so slight that calling it resistance is too strong, and then it is behind you and closed again, and you are on the other side.
I have gone down through it forty times now and every single time the words that arrive in my head, unbidden, before I have any say in the matter, are: that one’s been parted.
Not crossed. Parted.
And I have started counting them, going down. Three at the moment, in June. There was a fourth in April.
The last thing and then I will stop.
At fifty metres, with the black weighing on me and the grain going and the four seconds of nothing between the heartbeats, I put my hand up in front of my face.
I could not see it. That is not remarkable; there is no light, there is nothing to see it by.
What is remarkable is that I could not find it.

I knew where my hand was. I could feel my hand. I had put it there. But the place I felt my hand and the place I was looking were not the same place, and I moved it about for what was probably four or five seconds trying to get the two to agree, and they would not agree, and at some point in that four or five seconds a thought arrived that I am going to write down because I promised at the start of the fourth notebook that I would put everything in.
The thought was: how do I know it’s mine.

Not frightened. That is what I cannot get across and what I am not going to be able to get across to anybody, least of all a woman on the surface holding a stopwatch. There was no fear in it anywhere. It was a mild administrative question, of the sort you might have about a coat in a cloakroom.

Down there a man is being crushed at the chest and is bleeding a little into himself and cannot see any part of his own body and has no evidence, of any kind, in any sense, that he possesses one. There is a heartbeat the size of a hole in the moor and a grain that his own eyes are making and four seconds of nothing, over and over, and a question about a coat.
I have got to sixty and Sabine has put seventy on the plate for Sunday and I have asked for ninety-four, which is the floor, and she has not said no.
I do not think she is going to say no.
THIRTEEN. 55 METRES
From the log of Aurel Nizan. Fifth notebook. This entry is written in ink, which is the only entry in five notebooks that is.
There is somebody down there.
I have put off writing that sentence for six weeks and I want to record why, because the why is more interesting than the sentence.
It is not because I think it is untrue. It is because I have been protecting it.

I know exactly what happens if I say it out loud. I have been told what happens, in a hut, with a heater on, by a woman who had clearly rehearsed it. It is common. It is boring. It happens to climbers and to men in lifeboats and to people who walk across ice, and there is a literature, and it is the oldest trick the head has, and it means only that I am low and cold and deep. A reading on a gauge.

So the moment I say it, it stops being what it is and becomes an entry on a list of things that happen to people in my condition. And I have found that I do not want that. Not because I think the list is wrong. The list is almost certainly right. I do not want it because the list is nothing to do with what it is like, and once you have accepted the list you are no longer permitted to describe anything.
I would rather have the thing than the explanation of the thing. I am aware that is exactly what a man in my condition would write.
Facts first. Sabine’s rule and it is a good rule.

It arrives past thirty. Not at a depth exactly — it is not like the colour going, it has no timetable I can hold it to — but never above thirty and usually within a few seconds of the fall beginning. Eleven dives out of the last fourteen. The three where it did not come were the three where I was cold going in, which I think is a real correlation and which I offer without a theory.
It does not approach.

That is the first thing I want on the page and it is the most important. It does not swim up, or emerge, or come out of the dark, or any of the things that would be in a story. When I notice it, it is already there, and it is already falling, and it is already falling at exactly my rate.
Which means — and I have thought about this a great deal — that either it began falling when I began falling, or it has been falling the entire time and I have simply come alongside.
I cannot decide which of those is worse and I have stopped trying.
It is on my left. Always the left, all eleven times. About an arm’s length, a little below, so that if I turned my head I would be looking slightly down at it.
I do not turn my head.

I am going to write down what I know about what it looks like, and the reader of this notebook, if there ever is one, should understand that I have never once seen it, because there is no light at fifty-five metres and nothing is visible and I am not claiming to have seen anything.
I know it the way you know somebody is standing in your kitchen doorway behind you.
It is my size.

It is in the same attitude I am in — head down, arms in, legs together. Not similar. The same. When I adjust, it has already adjusted; there is no lag and no imitation, which is what makes copying the wrong word. A thing that copies you is a beat behind. This is not a beat behind. It is more like the two of us are being held in the same position by the same arrangement.
The only difference I have ever been able to identify is the strap.

I do not know why I know this. I have no explanation for how a man in absolute blackness comes to be certain about a length of rubber. But there is something trailing from its head — a mask strap, it must be a mask strap — and it is too long. It goes back and up past where the shoulder would be, drifting the wrong way against the fall, and it is longer than mine by a clear amount, and it is the only thing in eleven dives that has ever been wrong.
Everything else matches. That one thing is too long.
I have started, in the car afterwards, checking my own.
It has never touched me.

It has never spoken. I want to be careful here because “spoken” is a word that will be used against me. There is no voice. Nothing says anything. There is no communication of any kind that I could describe to a doctor.
There is only the attitude of it, and the attitude is patient.

I have known one patient person in my life. My grandmother, who came out of Oran in nineteen-fifty-something with two bags and a sister and never in eighty-one years hurried at anything, and who used to sit in a chair by a window with her hands in her lap for whole afternoons, entirely awake, waiting for nothing in particular. When I was nine that frightened me. I could not work out what she was doing and it did not seem to me that a person could be that still and be inside still.
It is that. It is exactly that, at fifty-five metres, in four-degree water, at an arm’s length on my left.
On the ninth dive it held something out.
I am going to write this plainly and then I am going to stop for the night.

The hand came up — the near hand, the left one from my point of view, which would be its right — and turned over, palm upward, and stopped. And there was something in the palm. Small. Not heavy. The shape was not a shape I recognised, and it was pale, which is a thing I have no business saying about an object in total darkness, and I am saying it anyway because it was pale.
And then nothing happened.

That is the whole event. It held something out and waited, and I did not take it, because I did not think of taking it, because the thought did not arrive, and I went on falling and it went on falling beside me and at sixty I put my hand on the plate and turned and came up and did the rite correctly on the surface and Sabine wrote down my time.
It has done it on every dive since. Nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen. The same hand. The same turn. The same pale small thing. The same waiting.

There is no pressure in it. I need that understood by anybody who ever reads this. It does not urge. It does not close the distance. It holds a thing out in a place where nothing can be seen and waits with the patience of a woman by a window for as long as I am there, and when I turn to go it does not follow and does not object.
The offer stays open. That is the shape of it. Not a demand — an offer, left standing, for as long as I care to leave it standing.
I have understood something in the last fortnight and I am putting it at the bottom where I can find it again.
I used to come down here for the fridge to be unplugged. For the voice to stop. I wrote that in the second notebook and it was true then.
The voice has not stopped in six weeks. The voice has gone, entirely, at any depth past thirty, and I no longer come down for the silence.

I come down because I have started to think that the offer will not stay open forever, and because I do not know what will happen when it closes, and because — and this is the thing I have not been able to say in sixteen months of writing in notebooks — I have begun to want to know what is in the hand.
Not to take it. To know.
Sabine has put seventy on the plate.
FOURTEEN. 60 METRES
Maude does not steal the notebook, which Sabine will think about later. She simply asks for it, in the car park, on a Saturday, in her professional voice, and Aurel hands it over.
“I’d like to photograph some pages,” Maude says. “For the file.”
“Which pages?”
“All of them.”
“All right,” he says.

She does it on the bonnet of her car, one page at a time, with her phone, in the flat white light of a June afternoon, ninety-odd pages, and it takes her forty minutes, and Aurel sits on the wall the whole time drinking tea out of a flask and does not read over her shoulder or ask what she wants it for.
Then she gives it back to him and drives to her sister’s house and puts the phone on the kitchen table.
“Read it,” she says.

Sabine reads it standing up. She reads it for an hour and ten minutes and does not sit down once, and at some point Maude makes tea that neither of them drinks, and at some point the light in the kitchen changes and neither of them puts a lamp on.

She reads about the red O-ring at five metres. She reads about the gun put down on the bench in the second month, and the fridge unplugged, and the sentence I have spent my entire life in an argument with myself. She reads the arithmetic, which is correct, and the account of the two lines that she drew herself on a page torn out of the sign-in book, transcribed accurately and understood better than she taught it.
She reads: You do not warn a man that carefully about a face in a curtain.
She reads the four not-colours between thirty-five and sixty. She reads the heart the size of the hole in the moor with four seconds of nothing between beats. She reads that one’s been parted.
She reads the hand held up at fifty metres and not found, and the mild administrative question about the coat in the cloakroom.
And then she reads eleven pages in ink and she gets to the strap.

Maude, from the other side of the table, will say afterwards that her sister made no sound at all and did not move, and that the only thing that happened was that she stopped reading for about fifteen seconds, in the middle of a page, with her eyes open.
“Well,” Maude says, when she has put the phone down.
“Well.”
“I’d like you to tell me what I’ve just given you.”
Sabine puts both hands flat on the table.
Here is what she could say, and she has all of it, she has had all of it for nine years and four papers’ worth of reading on top:

He is describing the standard picture. All of it. The presence at depth, the failure of attribution, the doubling. The head loses the ability to sign for its own material and hands the surplus to a category, and the category is a person, and the person is the diver himself because the diver is the only template available. It is in the literature. It has been in the literature since men started going into caves. Cold, dark, alone, running low, no reference — you will be given a companion, and the companion will be you, and it will be you because there is nothing else down there to build one out of.
All of that is true. She could say it in ninety seconds and it would be honest and complete and Maude, who is not a fool, would recognise it as an answer.
What she says is: “The strap.”
“What about it?”

“He’s never seen it. He says so. He says there’s no light and he’s not claiming to have seen anything. And then he tells you a length of rubber is wrong.” Sabine’s voice is quite level. “You don’t invent that, Maude. If your head is building you a companion out of whatever’s lying about, it builds you something significant. It builds you your mother. It builds you the man you owe money to. It does not build you an accurate copy of yourself and then put one detail wrong in it and leave the detail there for eleven dives.”
“Why not?”
“Because there’s nothing in it. There’s no meaning in a strap. It doesn’t do anything.” She looks up. “That’s not what a head makes. That’s what a thing looks like.”
Maude says nothing for a moment. Then: “Say the rest of it.”
“There is no rest of it.”
“Sabine.”
“There’s no rest of it,” Sabine says, and it is the first outright lie she has told her sister in nine years, and she tells it in a good clear voice with her hands flat on a table.
The seventy comes off the plate. She tells him on the Thursday and she does not explain, and she puts sixty back on, and she expects an argument and does not get one, which is worse.
“Sixty,” Aurel says. “All right.”
“You’re not going to ask why.”
“You’d give me a third of it.”
She almost laughs.

What she has decided — and she has decided it over three sleepless nights with a phone full of photographs of a young man’s handwriting — is that she is going to watch one more dive. That is all. One dive at sixty, with her at fifteen and the arithmetic on her wrist, and she is going to look at him properly on the way up, the way she has been avoiding looking at him all summer, and then she is going to make a decision.
She is aware, even while making this plan, that it is not a plan. It is a fortnight bought at retail.

He goes at 13:40 on the last Sunday in June and it is the ninth dive he has done past fifty metres and it is the one everybody in Ossay would tell you about afterwards if anybody in Ossay had been told.

Down in fifty-eight seconds. Fall from twenty-nine. Sabine holds at fifteen with her face out and one arm through the buoy strap and watches the line, and the line does the only thing the line ever does, which is be slightly less slack than it was.
At two twenty, which is early, the line moves.
She puts her face in.

He comes up out of the black at twenty-two metres and he comes up easily, on the same rhythm he went down on, and what she thinks — and she will write this down that night in her own hand because there is nobody in the world she can say it to — is that he looks like a man walking back up a garden path.
And then at eighteen metres he coughs.
Sabine sees it from fifteen and she sees all of it, and it is four seconds long, and it is the four seconds she will have for the rest of her life.
His body jolts — not a punch, she knows the punches, this is higher and it comes from the chest and it doubles him slightly — and his mouth opens, and something comes out of it.

It comes out slowly. That is the first wrong thing. It does not billow or spread; it leaves him in a thick unhurried rope and it hangs, and it turns over on itself once in the water in front of his face, and it holds together.
And it is black.

Absolutely black. Blacker than the water it is in — she can see it clearly, it is the darkest thing at eighteen metres, it reads against the grey the way ink reads on newsprint, and there is no red in it anywhere, and there cannot be, because red died at five metres and there is not one particle of it left in this hole to lend to anything.
He does not react.

He hangs there at eighteen metres in a hole in the moor with his own blood coming out of his mouth in a black rope, and he watches it, and he turns his head very slightly to keep watching it as it moves, and the expression on his face is one that Sabine has seen on exactly one other human being in her life, at a distance of two feet, on a slate ledge at the western end of this water, nine years ago in April, holding up a thermos like a trophy.
Then he closes his mouth and comes up.
Three breaths. Small, then larger, then larger.
Mask off — all the way off, not pushed up. Eyes: he finds hers and holds them for a full three seconds. Hand out of the water. Thumb and forefinger. Circle.
“I’m okay.”

Sabine gets to him and takes his jaw in her hand and turns his face and there is a thin dark line at the corner of his mouth, drying already, going red now that it is up in the air where red is allowed, and she says, “You’re bleeding,” and he says, “I know,” and she says, “How long has that been happening,” and Aurel Nizan, treading water with steady eyes and a good pulse and no shakes at all, says:
“Since April.”
He is not evading. He does not think he has done anything. He answers in the voice of a man who has been asked how long he has had that cough.
“April,” Sabine says.

“It doesn’t hurt. It comes up and then it stops.” He wipes his mouth with the back of his wrist, and looks at the wrist, and something crosses his face — and it is not fear, and it is not shame, and she will spend the rest of the summer failing to find a better word for it than sorrow. “It’s the wrong colour on the surface,” he says.
Then he says, “Sixty next week?”
FIFTEEN. 70 METRES
Maude does the reading on the Monday, which is what she does instead of sleeping.

She has a page from a diving forum, four years old, and two papers she has paid for out of her own account, and by two in the morning she can say it in her own words, which is the only test she trusts.

Past about thirty metres a chest gets squeezed smaller than it can go. Not smaller than full — smaller than empty, smaller than it goes when you have breathed everything out and pushed and there is nothing left. There is a floor to how small a chest can be made, and the water goes through the floor, and after the floor something has to give, and what gives is the smallest vessels in the lungs. They leak. What leaks is blood, and it gets into the space where the air is supposed to be, and later it comes up.

It is not exotic. That is what stops her. She had expected something rare and it is not rare at all — every competitive diver in the world has had a touch of it, half of them cough on the boat and say nothing, and there is an entire culture of saying nothing that the papers refer to, drily, as underreporting.
And it is not a sign of one dive going wrong.

That is the sentence she reads four times. You do not get this because a dive went badly. You get it because forty dives went well. It is the bill for a season, not for an afternoon, and it arrives quietly in a young man who feels excellent and whose numbers are all improving.

Aurel Nizan has been leaking since April, by his own admission, on a site her employer insures, under the supervision of a coach her employer engaged on her own recommendation, whose report she will be assessing in nine days.
At half past two she writes the position out plainly, because she has learned that she cannot lie to a document as easily as she can lie to herself.

I can end this on Wednesday. One letter to the lease-holder and one to the council and the gate gets a padlock that means something, and he never sees that water again. Exposure goes to nil. My employer’s interest is served. My professional duty is discharged in a morning.
I will not do it.
I will not do it because he will drive to a reservoir, which is true, and which I have been using as a reason since March, and which is not the reason.

The reason is that in nine days I am going to be handed a document in my sister’s handwriting about the fourth of April, and if I bar him now there is no document, and the file closes, and I go the rest of my life without being told.

I have been describing myself for nine years as a woman who wants to know what happened. I am not sure that is what I am. I think I am a woman who has arranged for it to keep not happening, so that the asking never has to end.
She reads that back, and does not delete it, and puts the file away at three.
She goes to the house that night.

Sabine has the good lamp on and the kitchen table covered: the tables, the four notebooks copied out longhand into a fifth in her own writing, a page of arithmetic done three times, and the phone face down.
“I’ve been reading about lungs,” Maude says.
“I know. You rang the club at Rennes on Saturday and they rang me.”
“Then you know what I’m going to say.”
“I know that too.”
Maude sits down without being asked, which she has not done in this kitchen for nine years, and takes her glasses off, and rubs the bridge of her nose.
“Then let’s do this properly,” she says. “Because I’ve got about eleven days and then I have to write something down, and once I’ve written it down it’s a fact about the world.”
“All right.”
“The report. Are you going to sign it?”
“I’m going to write the truth in it.”

“That’s not what I asked and you know it isn’t.” Maude puts the glasses back on. “You are going to write, in a document that goes into a file that outlives all three of us, that the water at the Cut is satisfactorily managed. And nine days after that, that boy is going to ask you for ninety-four metres, and you are going to be holding the watch.”
“He’s twenty-six.”

“He’s a boy, Sabine, he works nights making clips, he taught himself out of library books, he’s been on his own in a hole for seventeen months and he found somebody at the bottom of it who’s patient with him, and you have read what he wrote, and I have watched your face while you read it.” Maude’s voice does not rise. It does the opposite; it goes down and flattens, the way it does with claimants who are about to be caught. “You know what he’s describing. Don’t tell me it’s in the literature. I’ve read the literature, I’ve read more of it than you have, I’ve had nine years and a subscription. You know what he’s describing because you have been there.”
“Maude—”
“’There was somebody there and it was not her.’”
The kitchen goes very quiet.
“You’ve got the statement,” Sabine says.

“I’ve had the statement since the week it was taken. I’ve read it two hundred times. I’ve read it more than I’ve read anything.” Maude is completely steady now. “And I have never once asked you about that sentence, in nine years, and do you know why? Because I decided early on that if I asked you and you lied to me, I’d have nothing left. So I kept it in a file and I built round it. I built a very good case. It’s got sixty-one items in it.”
“A case for what?”

“That you were negligent,” Maude says. “That the line was rigged the night before and left overnight and neither of you checked it. That you did four dives at increasing depth with no medic and no third person on the surface. That you knew she was going for seventy-two and you held the surface anyway when you should have said no, and that you had said no to her once before, in February, and she’d sulked for a week, and you didn’t fancy the week.”
Sabine says nothing.

“That’s the case. Sixty-one items. It’s airtight and it’s nine years old and I have never once submitted it anywhere, and last month I finally worked out why.” Maude looks at her sister across a kitchen table. “It’s not because I love you. Let’s be honest for one evening. It’s because it’s not the crime.”
“Maude.”

“Every item’s true and the whole thing’s wrong. I’ve known that for years and I’ve kept adding to it anyway, because a wrong case that you can finish is worth more than a right question you can’t ask.” She takes a breath. “So I’m asking. Once. Tonight. And then never again, and I mean never, I’m too tired.
“What did you mean, there was somebody there and it was not her?”

And Sabine Vasseur, forty-four years old, nine years dry, with four notebooks copied out in her own hand on the table in front of her, looks at her sister and understands with absolute clarity that this is the moment — that it is here, that it has arrived early, that she could put it down right now on a Monday night in a kitchen with the good lamp on, and that everything after would be different and slower and survivable.
“Nothing,” she says. “I was gone.”
Maude sits very still.
Then she nods, once, and puts her hands on the table and pushes herself up out of the chair like a woman twenty years older.
“Right,” she says.
At the door she stops.

“He’ll get to ninety-four,” she says, not turning round. “You know he will. And when he comes up from it you’ll have your hand on his jaw looking at his eyes, and he’ll do the four things, and he’ll do them perfectly, because he does everything perfectly, and you’ll write his time down.”
“Yes.”
“And you’ll know.”
“Yes,” Sabine says.

“That’s what I can’t—” Maude stops. Starts again. “Nine years I’ve thought you couldn’t go near that water because of what it took off you. And I’ve spent this month watching you get a suit out for a boy with a notebook, and Sabine, I’ll tell you what it looks like from the top of the ramp.
“It looks like you’re waiting to find out what he says yes to.”
She lets herself out.
Sabine stays at the table until the boiler goes off.

Then she goes to the cupboard under the stairs and comes back with the mask and puts it down on the kitchen table among the notebooks and the arithmetic, and sits with her hands flat either side of it, and does not touch it again all night.

From the log of Aurel Nizan. Sixth notebook, first page. The hand is completely even and there are no corrections anywhere in the entry.
Sabine did not put ninety-four on the plate. I want that recorded first because it matters and because there will be people afterwards who need it to be otherwise.

She put seventy on the plate. She rigged the line to seventy-eight herself, twice checked, and she told me seventy and she told me the arithmetic and I said it back to her and I had it exactly. She was at fifteen with a lanyard on. There were two medics on the platform from the club forty miles off, who came because she rang them on the Wednesday and asked them to, which I do not think she has ever done for anybody.
She did everything correctly. She has done everything correctly since April. If there is a form to be filled in afterwards, the form will say that the water was managed.
I went to the floor because I decided to, at about sixty-two metres, on my own, with nobody’s permission.
The fall started at twenty-eight, which is the earliest yet.
I passed her at fifteen. I remember her hand come out and touch my shoulder as I went by, which is what she does, and which she has done on every dive since April, and I remember being glad about it.
Then the last of the green went and I was in it.

The layers: three. Forty-three, and then something small at about fifty-one that I have not felt before, and then the deep one at sixty which is the coldest thing in the hole and which I have written about as being like putting your face against a window in winter.
All three parted.

They parted the way they always part — the contact across the whole face at once and the almost-nothing of resistance and then behind me and closed again. And I counted them, because I always count them, and after the third one I was at sixty-two metres and I understood, with no drama about it at all, that there was nothing left to part.
That is how I knew. Not a feeling. An absence of the next thing.

Past sixty-two the water did not change temperature again. Not once, not by any amount, all the way down. Thirty-two more metres of water at exactly one temperature, with no edge in it anywhere, and nothing between me and the floor.
I have been going down through curtains for seventeen months.
There were no more curtains.
It was already there when the fall began, as always, on my left, a little below, and it fell at my rate all the way, and past sixty-two it came closer.
Not quickly. There was nothing sudden in it. It closed the distance the way water closes: continuously, without any moment you could point to.
By eighty metres it was an arm’s length. By ninety it was less than that.
At the floor we were side by side.
The floor.

There is nothing there. I want to be very clear about this because everybody wants there to be something. Sabine says people always want the bottom of the water to be a museum. She is right and I have wanted it too — I have imagined the winch and the rails and the cart for seventeen months, in bed, before sleep, the way you imagine a room you have not been into.

There is silt. It is deep and it is very fine and it holds the shape of a hand for a long time, which I know because I put a hand into it. There is broken slate. There is the plate at the end of the line, which was not there, because the line was rigged to seventy-eight and I was at ninety-four.
That is the entire inventory of the bottom of the Cut. Silt, slate, and the fact of being there.

And the black at ninety-four is not the black at fifty. I have written about four not-colours between thirty-five and sixty and I have written that the timetable does not end, and I was right, it does not end, and what is at the floor is the last one and there will not be another.
There is no grain in it.

That is the difference and it is the whole difference. At fifty metres my own eyes were still making static for me — the last manufactured thing, I called it, and I was proud of the phrase. At ninety-four the static has stopped. I do not know why and I do not think anybody knows why. My eyes were open. There was nothing coming in and nothing going on and nothing being made.
I have spent my whole life inside a certain amount of noise and I have written in these notebooks about the fridge being unplugged, and I thought I knew what quiet was, and I did not.
Nothing is happening. Nothing has ever happened. Nothing is going to.

I have read about the men who sit in caves for years to arrive at a thing they will not describe afterwards, and I used to find that a sort of showing off. I do not now. I think they got there and found it was not describable and came out and had to say something to the people who had brought them food.

I was at the floor of a quarry in the north of a small department for perhaps eleven seconds and I was not lonely, and I was not frightened, and I was not anything, and the argument I have been having with myself since I was a child was not paused or quiet or under control.
It had never happened.
Then it turned to face me.

Fourteen months, forty-odd dives, and it has never once altered its attitude. Head down, arms in, exactly as I am, never a beat behind, never imitating, held in the same position by the same arrangement.
At the floor it turned to face me.

I am not going to write that I saw it. There was no light of any kind and there is nothing at ninety-four metres to see anything by. But I knew what was in front of me the way you know the shape of your own kitchen in the dark, and what was in front of me was myself, at an arm’s length, in four degrees of water, at the bottom of a hole, facing me.

Same size. Same build. Same set of the shoulders. The scar across the back of the left hand from the guard on the moulding machine in the second week of the job, which I have not written about in any notebook and which is the only mark on my body that nobody but me could have put there.
And the strap, going back and up, drifting the wrong way, too long.
The hand came up.

The same hand as always, the near one, and it turned over, palm upward, and there was the small pale thing in it. Not heavy. I have never had a word for the shape and I do not have one now. Pale, which I have no business saying, and I am saying it.
And it did not wait.

That is the only thing I want to put down about what happened next, and I have thought about it for four days, and I have written this entry in one sitting with no crossings-out because I have had four days to decide what I am willing to write.

In seventeen months it has never once urged and never once closed the distance and never once followed me up, and the offer has stayed open, standing, patient, for as long as I cared to leave it standing. And I wrote in the fifth notebook that I had begun to think the offer would not stay open forever, and I did not know how I knew that, and I still do not.
At the floor it did not wait.
The hand came up and turned over and it was not being offered to me any more.
It was being given.
I got to the surface. I did the four things. I did them correctly: three breaths, mask all the way off, her eyes for three seconds, the circle, and I said the words.

My time was five minutes and fifty-eight seconds and my depth was ninety-four metres and both of those numbers are impossible and Sabine wrote them down without her hand shaking, which I noticed, and which I have thought about since.
I am not going to write down whether I took it.

I have been putting everything in these notebooks for seventeen months. Everything, including the tablets, including the fridge, including the coat in the cloakroom, including a length of rubber I could not possibly have seen.
I am not putting this in.

Not because I am ashamed and not because I have decided to keep a secret from a notebook, which would be a stupid thing to do. It is because I have gone over the eleven seconds at the floor perhaps four hundred times in four days, in the car and at the machine and lying awake, and I cannot find the moment.
There is the hand coming up.
There is the surface.
There is nothing in between, and there has never been anything in between, and I have looked.
I know that I agreed to something. I know it the way you know you have signed for a parcel. And I cannot get back to the place where the pen was.
