SEVENTEEN. 94 → 60 METRES
From the log of Aurel Nizan. Sixth notebook, second entry. Written eleven days after the first.
There is a thing I did not put in the last entry because I had not noticed it yet.
Coming up is not coming up.

I have done a hundred and eleven dives and until the floor I would have said that a dive has two halves and the second half is the expensive one. You go down, which is free after thirty metres, and then you turn, and then you pay. That is the shape of it. Sabine draws it as a line going down across a page and she is right and every book agrees with her.
From ninety-four metres it was not a line going down.

I turned. I know I turned, because I was at the floor with my hand in the silt and then I was not. And what happened between the floor and about sixty metres was not effort and not ascent and not anything I can put a verb to.
It was a discussion.

I want to be careful, because I have already written that nothing speaks down there and that remains true. There was no voice, no words, nothing that could be repeated. But there is a kind of exchange that happens between two people over a table when a thing has already been settled and all that is left is the terms — who carries what, what gets kept, what is going to be said afterwards — and that is the closest I can get to what happened between the floor and the deep cold layer at sixty.
I have been in that conversation before. I had it with the woman I lived with for three years, in a kitchen, in the last week, when we both already knew and were only working out the furniture.
At sixty metres I came through the deep cold layer. It was there again — it had been gone on the way down, and coming up it was back, and it parted the way it always parts, and it closed behind me.

And past it I was swimming, and it was costing me, and everything after that was the ordinary bill in the ordinary currency. Sixty to the surface as a man. Punches from about fifty. Six pairs. The last twenty metres hard.
The other one did not come up past sixty.

I want that on the page. Below sixty it was beside me the whole way and above sixty it was not, and I did not look for it, and I was not sad about it, and it did not occur to me until I was in the car that anything had ended.
I want to record one more thing about the discussion, because it is the only part of it I can put a shape to.
At some point in the thirty-four metres between the floor and the deep cold layer, I did the inventory.

That is Sabine’s word and it is her method and she taught it to me on the surface in June when I was trying to relax by effort and she told me that relaxation is not a mood, it is plumbing — that you go through yourself part by part and find what is switched on that does not need to be, and switch it off. A jaw slightly set. A hand slightly closed. A shoulder up round the ear because the water is four degrees. She said all of it is spending and all of it gets paid for at depth in a currency you cannot see the balance of.
I have done the inventory on every dive since June. It takes about eight seconds and by July I could do it without thinking.
Coming up from the floor I did it, and I got to the end of it, and everything was off.

Everything. Jaw, hands, shoulders, the whole cage, the small muscles round the eyes that nobody ever finds on the first hundred attempts. Not one thing in me was doing anything it had not been asked to do, and I was not making it happen, and it had not taken eight seconds, it had already been true when I started looking.

I have worked for four months at a skill that Sabine says takes most divers years and some divers never, and on the way up from ninety-four metres I found it finished. Completed. Handed back to me done.
That is the first thing in seventeen months that I have wanted to give back.
Sabine’s account of the same dive, which she gave me on the Wednesday, in the hut, reading off a page:

Down in one minute nine to sixty-two. Then nothing on the watch for a very long time. She had told me seventy and rigged to seventy-eight and she went at three fifty, which is what she said she would do, and she got to thirty-one metres, and she says that is as far as she could get, and I believe her.
She came up empty at four twenty.
I surfaced at five fifty-eight.

She says that between four twenty and five fifty-eight she was on the surface with a hand on the buoy strap and one of the medics holding her wrist, and that she did not shout and did not send the second medic down and did not do any of the four things that she has spent twenty-two years teaching people to do in exactly that situation.
I asked her why not.
She said: “Because you weren’t in trouble.”
I said: “How could you know that?”

And she looked at the page for a while and then she said, “I’ve been at fifteen metres under you thirty-one times. I know what you feel like in the water when you’re working. There was nothing in that water that was working.”

That is not an answer that would survive an inquiry. She knows that. She wrote it down on the page in front of her while she was saying it, in her own hand, and then she signed the page and dated it, which she has done after every dive since April, and which I have only this week understood is not paperwork.
She is building a record. Deliberately. Of everything she has seen and every decision she has made and every reason she had at the time.
I asked her who it was for.
She said, “My sister.”
Now the thing I have to write down, and I have put it at the end because I do not know what to do with it.
On the Thursday I did not go to see my mother.

I go on Thursdays. I have gone on Thursdays for six years, since the stroke, and it is forty minutes each way and she does not always know who I am and it does not matter, and I have never once minded going. That is not me being good. I want that clear. I have minded almost everything I have ever had to do and I have never minded that, and I used to think it was because the argument in my head went quiet in her room, the way it goes quiet in the water, and I now think it was simpler than that. I liked her. I like her.
On Thursday I finished at six and drove home and made food and read for two hours and went to bed.

I did not forget. That is the part. I have gone over it and there was no moment of forgetting — I did not think I will go later and then not go. I knew it was Thursday. I knew what Thursdays are. The knowledge was fully available to me all evening, in the way that the knowledge that there is a coat in a cupboard is available to you.
It simply did not come with anything attached.

I have sat with this for four days and the honest description is that I read the fact of it off the inside of my own head the way you read a note somebody else has left on a table. Thursday. Mother. And nothing moved. No pull, no guilt, no reluctance, not even the small mean relief of getting out of something. There was no pressure in it in either direction.
Six years of Thursdays and it had gone completely flat.
I went on the Friday instead and it was fine and she knew me for about ten minutes and I sat and held her hand.
And here is what frightens me, and it is not the missed evening.

Sitting there holding her hand I noticed that I was doing it correctly. Thumb across the back of the knuckles, the way she likes. Talking about the weather in the town, which is the only subject that reliably lands. Not too loud. All of it exactly right, all of it performed to a standard I have never once had to think about in six years.
Thinking about it is new.

I have written a hundred pages in these notebooks about the fridge being unplugged and the argument stopping and the seconds losing their edges, and I have been treating all of that as an unqualified good, and it has cost me nothing so far, and I have said so in writing more than once.
It has started costing.

The thing at the bottom of the Cut is not frightened, and is not lonely, and is not in an argument with itself, and is patient in a way that no living person has ever managed for more than an afternoon. I have wanted to be that for seventeen months.
I am only now working out what would have to be taken out of a man to make him like that.
Not the fear. The fear is the small part.
You would have to take out everybody.

ITEM 62. The bloodwork.
I obtained it lawfully and I want the method recorded because the method is going to matter if anybody ever reads this file who is not me.

A. Nizan attended the occupational health provider retained by his employer on 3 July for a routine two-yearly assessment which he was due in any case. He asked them, at the appointment, to run a fuller panel than the one they were going to run, and he told them why, and he signed a release permitting the results to be sent to me.
He did not have to do that. I asked and I expected him to say no.
He said — and I wrote it down in the car park afterwards because I wanted it exactly — “You should have it. Somebody should have it who’s going to be difficult about it.”
I have thought about that sentence more than is useful.
ITEM 63. What is in the blood that should not be.
Four things, and they are all the same kind of thing.

There are proteins that live inside the cells of a brain and are not supposed to be anywhere else. They belong on the other side of a wall — there is a barrier between the blood and the brain, and it is a good barrier, and its whole purpose is that the two do not mix. When those proteins turn up in a blood sample it means the wall has been leaky.
They are the markers you would run on a man who had been hit in the head.
All four are up in A. Nizan.

I have had this looked at twice. The first doctor I asked said it was consistent with severe strain and probably transient and that she would want a second sample in three months. The second, a man in Brest who has published on breath-hold divers and who spoke to me for fifty minutes for nothing, said something more useful.

He said the wall goes leaky in these divers routinely and it is measurable after a single hard hold and that this is known and not disputed. He said the honest state of the field is that nobody knows what it adds up to over years, because the sport is thirty years old and the people who would tell you are still alive.
Then he said: “Ask me what I actually worry about.”
I asked.
He said: “Not the blood. I worry about the ones who feel better.”
ITEM 64. The contradiction.
Here is what I cannot make resolve, and I have been trying for eleven days, and I am writing it down as a contradiction rather than pretending I have solved it.
Column one. Injury.

Blood in the lungs since April, by his own admission, witnessed once at twenty-two metres in front of my sister. Four brain proteins elevated where none should be. A left ear that has been giving him trouble since May and which he has not had looked at. A hundred and eleven dives in seventeen months, thirty-one of them past forty metres, nine past sixty, and one to the floor.
By every measure I am professionally equipped to apply, this is a man being taken apart.
Column two. Function.

His resting heart rate has come down eleven beats in four months. His hold on the surface has gone from five minutes twenty to six minutes forty. The depth at which his chest closes and he stops swimming has moved from thirty-one metres in April to twenty-eight in July, which the man in Brest tells me is a real adaptation and not a measurement error and takes most divers years.

He needs less rest between dives than he did in the spring. That is backwards. My sister has said this to me three times in three different tones of voice and I did not understand until this month that she was not admiring it.

And there has not been one single episode. Not one. In a hundred and eleven dives, not once has he come up shaking, and roughly one dive in ten ends that way at the top of this sport under judges with medics on a platform. My sister has had it four times in her life. Elvire Baudry had it eleven times and kept count of them at the back of a logbook, one mark apiece, apparently because she found it amusing.
By every measure available, this is a man in the best condition of his life.
Both columns are correct. I have checked the numbers three times. They are not in tension because one of them is wrong. They are simultaneously true.
I have a young man whose lungs are bleeding and whose brain is leaking and who is getting better.
ITEM 64b. The training record.
She has given me the training book, unasked, on 6 July. Hardback, bought in April, ninety-one pages, and she has put her signature and the date at the foot of every one of them.

I have assessed a great many training records in eleven years and most of them are written to survive an inquiry. Hers is not. It is worse than that. It is written by somebody who knew from the beginning that there would be an inquiry and decided to be the person who wrote everything down first.

The programme itself is conservative to the point of timidity and I want that stated plainly because it is the single most inconvenient fact in this entire file. She found him at thirty-one metres in April and would not let him past forty until the end of May. Depth increases of five metres. Two enforced rest days a week. Eleven weeks of remedial work on his ears at five metres over a bench, which he hated and which she made him do anyway. Chest and rib work twice a week on wet concrete in the rain. Dry tables logged daily, including — and this is unusual enough that I checked it against three other coaches — including every round he failed, which she required him to record and which most coaches do not.
There is a full rescue drill on 4 May. Both directions. She let him tow her.

I do not know what to do with that entry. She has written it up in four flat lines and she has signed it, and I have read the four lines perhaps thirty times. My sister has not been carried in that water since a man with a dog got her out of it nine years ago, and on 4 May she got into it and went limp on purpose and let a twenty-six-year-old man she had known six weeks take her jaw in his hand.
Under outcome she has written: drill completed correctly, all four steps. Diver competent.
She has written nothing about herself.
ITEM 64c. What the record does not contain.
Nothing. That is the finding and it took me nine days to arrive at it and I resent it.

There is no negligence in the training book. There is no corner cut, no number inflated, no rest day skipped, no unlogged session, no depth she cannot defend on the day she set it. If I put that book in front of a coaching board in Europe they would find it exemplary, and several of them would ask her to teach.
Every single thing she did was correct.

And the boy is bleeding into his lungs and leaking four proteins across a wall in his head and getting better, and the book that records how it happened is the best document of its kind I have ever read.

I have spent nine years assembling a case that she was careless. I have now read ninety-one signed pages proving that she was not, and it has not made me feel better for one minute, because carelessness was never what I was looking for and I have known that since about the fourth year.
ITEM 65. The wrong frame.
I spent the first week on this trying to make it a case of harm, because harm is what I do, and a file that establishes harm is a file that closes.

It will not go. Every time I write it up as harm I have to explain away column two, and column two will not be explained away; it is the strongest part of the evidence and it points the wrong direction.
So on Tuesday night I did the thing you are not supposed to do, which is put the columns side by side and stop trying to make one of them the error.

If a machine came into my office in this condition — parts failing, output rising — I would not write this machine is breaking down. I would write this machine is being run past its design and something is compensating, and my next question would be what, and my question after that would be what the compensation is being paid for with.
I do not have the second answer. I want that on the record. I have no theory and I am not going to invent one for a file.

But I have the first answer as a shape, and the shape is that something is holding him together while he is used, and that the holding-together is what shows up in column two, and that it is a service being performed and not a strength he has developed.
And that services are paid for.
ITEM 66. What he said on 3 July.
Standing in a car park with a release form in his hand.
I asked him — badly, because I had not planned to ask it — whether he had considered that he might be being harmed.
He said: “I’m not being harmed. That’s the whole problem.”
I said I did not understand.
And he said, and I am confident of this because I wrote it in the car within a minute: “If it was hurting me I’d stop. Everyone stops when it hurts. That’s what hurting is for.”
Then he said: “Ask your sister what happens when it doesn’t.”
ITEM 67. The declaration.
The form has been in my drawer since February.
I filled it in on Wednesday. I dated it, and I signed it, and I put it back in the drawer.

That is not a joke and it is not indecision. I want the file to show that on 9 July I completed a declaration of interest in this matter and did not submit it, and that I have kept it signed and dated where I can see it, so that on the day I do submit it there is no version of events in which I discovered my conflict late.

The report comes to me on Monday. It will be seventeen pages, because she has told me it will be seventeen pages. She has been writing it in longhand for six weeks in a kitchen at a table with a lamp on, and she has been signing and dating a page after every single dive since April, and she told me in June that the record was for me, and I did not believe her, and I believe her now.
I am going to read it and I am going to assess it honestly and I am going to write down whatever it makes me write down.

And then, on the Sunday after, he is going to ask her for ninety-four metres again, and she is going to give it to him, and I am going to be standing at the top of the ramp where I have stood for nine years.
ITEM 68. Action.
None available.

I want that in the file too. Sixty-eight items over nine years and the honest entry under action is none available, because everything I could do makes it worse, and the only thing that would work is a sentence from my sister that she has refused to say twice.
NINETEEN. 20 METRES
The report is seventeen pages and Maude reads it in her own kitchen on the Monday night with the declaration of interest signed and dated in a drawer twenty miles away.

Sixteen of the pages are the best professional document she has read in eleven years. Water temperature by depth by month, going back four years, taken by hand. Wall condition with photographs. The line rig, drawn to scale, with the failure modes numbered. A section on access that recommends, in the flat prose of a woman who knows what she is doing, that the site be closed to unaccompanied divers by physical means rather than by signage, because signage at this site has been tested for nine years and does not work.

There is a section headed Diver A which runs four pages and gives every depth, every time, every surface interval, the blood in the lungs, the four proteins, and the missed rest days, and which concludes that the diver in question is beyond the capacity of the site to supervise and should be diving under a full club structure with a medic on the platform, and that the coach’s continued supervision of him at the Cut is not defensible on the evidence and is nonetheless what is happening.
She has written that. About herself. In a document going into a file that outlives all three of them.
And then there is page seventeen.
Page seventeen is headed Annex: Statement of the author’s interest, and it is in the same hand as the other sixteen and it is not a professional document at all.
Maude reads it standing up at the counter with her coat still on.

I was offered something at the bottom of this water on the fourth of April nine years ago and I refused it, and I have never told anybody, and I am telling it here because my sister is going to read it and because I have run out of other ways to get it to her.
Elvire went at 11:31 for seventy-two metres. I held the surface. At about three minutes I knew — and I am not going to defend the word knew, I knew — and I went down after her.

I got to somewhere past fifty metres. I have never been able to give a number and I have stopped trying. It was the deepest I have ever been and it was the fastest I have ever gone and I was empty when I got there and I want that understood before anything else: I was, by every measure, a woman who was about to die.
She was not there.
Something was there.

It was on my left, a little below, and it was already there when I arrived, and it was not approaching and it did not have to, and it was me. My size, my build, my attitude in the water, and the only thing wrong with it in any particular was the strap, which was too long, and which went back and up and drifted the wrong way against the fall.
It held out its hand with something in it, palm up, and it waited.

I have had nine years to work out what was in the hand and I am no further on than I was in the water. I can tell you what it was not. It was not air and it was not Elvire and it was not a way out. It was not being rescued. Nothing about it was rescue.

The nearest I can get is this. I was thirty-five years old, at fifty-something metres, on nothing, four minutes in, with a woman I loved dead or dying somewhere below me, and I was being offered the thing that would mean none of that was pressing.
Not comfort. Not forgetting. The removal of the property that makes a thing press on you.

And I understood — completely, without being told, in the way you understand the shape of your own kitchen in the dark — that I could have it, and that having it was not free, and that what it cost was everybody.
I said no.

There were no words. I want to be accurate. There was nothing said by anybody. But there is no other honest verb for what I did and I have tried for nine years to find one. I was offered a thing and I declined it and then I turned round and swam up and left Elvire Baudry at sixty-eight metres, and I have signed a great many documents since and this is the first true one.

I did not come up because I was brave. I came up because I am small and frightened and I wanted my sister’s telephone number to keep mattering to me, and I have never been able to make that sound like a virtue and I have stopped trying.
Here is the part that is the actual point of this annex, and I have taken sixteen pages to arrive at it because I have been a coward about it since February.
It was never withdrawn.

That is what nine years have been. Not grief. Not guilt — I have plenty of guilt and it is the ordinary kind and I can carry it up a hill. The reason I have not put my face in that water since the fourth of April is not that I cannot bear to remember what happened in it.
It is that the offer is still open, and it is still down there, and it is patient, and water is the only place where I would have to see it again.

I have stood at the edge of it four hundred times and put one hand in and taken it out. I have told you that was a habit. It is not a habit. It is a man looking through a window at a shop he has decided not to go into, and doing it every day for nine years, and calling it a walk.

And in April a young man came out of that water and said six words to me on the surface — they don’t feel like mine — which are almost exactly the words I said to Elvire in a car in March nine years ago with a bag of chips on the handbrake, and she laughed, and I laughed, because at the time it was funny.
I have known since the twenty-sixth of April what he was going to meet.

I have taught him, since then, correctly, patiently, safely, everything he needed in order to get deep enough to meet it. Every lesson I gave him was true. Every number I put on that plate was defensible on the day I put it there. I have not lied to him once and I have not told him one thing that mattered, and if you put my conduct since April in front of any coaching board in Europe they would find nothing to strike me for, and they would be wrong.
Maude, you asked me twice.

You asked me in a corridor when I was thirty-five and I said nothing, I was gone, and you asked me at my own table in June and I said the same four words nine years later, and both times you took it and did not push, and I have spent nine years being grateful to you for not pushing and telling myself that gratitude was love.
It was not. It was relief.
Here is why I did not tell you, and it is the last thing and then the annex is finished and you can do what you like with it.

If I told you, it stopped being a thing that happened to me and became a thing about me. You would have taken it somewhere. You would have taken it to a doctor, which you did anyway with the two sentences you had, and the doctor would have been kind and correct and would have explained to me what a brain does at fifty metres with nothing in it, and I have read all of that, I have read more of it than you have, and it is all true.

And I would have had to believe it. That is what I could not have. Because if it is true — if it was a face in a curtain and nothing else — then I did not decline anything on the fourth of April. There was nothing to decline. I simply came up, the way a body comes up, and left her there, and the nine years are not a refusal held under pressure.
They are just nine years.
I needed it to have been an offer, because if it was an offer then I said no to it, and if I said no to it then leaving her was a choice a person made and not a thing a body did.
So I have needed, for nine years, for somebody else to be offered it. Somebody I did not put in the water, who came to it on his own, out of books, in a hole in the moor, without me.
And in April one arrived.
I have not pushed him one metre deeper than he was going anyway. I want that on the record and I believe it is true and I have checked it against the numbers and the numbers support me.

And I have watched him go down there forty times with a watch in my hand, and I have written down his times in a good clear hand, and every single time he has come up and done the four things correctly and looked me in the eye and said I’m okay, I have felt something that I am going to name here because this is the only document I am ever going to be honest in.
Disappointment.
I am forty-four years old and I have wanted, since the twenty-sixth of April, to find out whether anybody else would have said yes.
S. Vasseur. 13 July.
Maude stands at the counter for a long time.

Then she picks up her phone and does not ring her sister. She rings the number she has for A. Nizan and it goes to nothing, because he is on nights, because it is Monday, because he will be standing at a machine in a building on the Ossay road making clips until six in the morning with his phone in a locker.
She leaves no message.

She sits down at her own kitchen table at half past eleven at night with a seventeen-page report in front of her and a signed declaration of interest in a drawer twenty miles away, and she understands, with the flat clarity of a woman who has spent nine years building sixty-one items into an airtight case, that every item is true and the whole thing is worthless, and that the crime is not negligence, and never was.
It is that her sister has been waiting.
She opens the file and starts a new entry and writes, at the top, in her ordinary hand:
ITEM 69. She told me.
And then she cannot write anything else for a very long time, because the second thing she has understood, sitting there, is that she is not going to submit the declaration in the morning either.
She has waited nine years to be told. She has been told.
And there is one Sunday left, and Sunday is the only place where anybody is going to find out whether it was true.
TWENTY. 10 METRES
The word arrives on a Thursday, in a footnote, in the wrong document.

Maude is not looking for it. She has stopped looking; that is the point of the week. She has read her sister’s annex nine times, and she has read the four papers the man in Brest sent her, and she has done what she does, which is establish whether a thing has been described before.
It has. Repeatedly. Well.

The literature on being accompanied is not thin and it is not fringe. It is in mountaineering, where the men who have written about it are not the kind of men who write about anything. It is in polar work. It is in the accounts of people who came off boats and were in the water for a long time. There is a whole shelf of it and there is a name for it that comes out of an expedition across an island in the southern ocean, where three men crossed on foot in nineteen-sixteen and all three of them believed, separately and without discussing it, that a fourth had walked with them. One of them wrote it down. A poet stole it four years later and put it in a poem that Maude had to learn part of at school and had never once understood.

She reads for four days and by the Wednesday she has the shape of it. Cold, exhaustion, monotony, isolation, and a brain that has been given nothing to work on will produce a companion. It is not a symptom of anything wrong. It appears to be what the machinery does when it is run in a vacuum, and the people it happens to are, almost without exception, unshakeably certain at the time and mildly embarrassed afterwards.
Her sister is not embarrassed. Nine years and she has not moved an inch.
The footnote is in a paper about a different sport entirely.

It is a medical review of breath-hold diving injuries, published in a journal she has no business having access to and got anyway, and it is dry to the point of hostility, and on page nine there is a paragraph about historical populations of working divers.

The paragraph concerns the women who dived for shellfish on a particular stretch of Japanese coast, for centuries, without equipment, in cold water, several times a day, for their entire working lives. They went down on one breath and came up and went down again, and they did it into their seventies, and there were thousands of them, and they are the largest population of habitual breath-hold divers in the recorded history of the species.
And they had a word for it.

Maude reads the paragraph twice and then goes and finds the source, which takes her two days and a librarian in Rennes and forty euros: a collection of oral accounts gathered in the nineteen-thirties by a folklorist who spent years on that coast writing down what the divers told him, published in 1939, and translated into French in the sixties by somebody who did the work well and put a long apologetic preface on the front about how much he had failed to carry over.
There are twelve accounts.
The word is tomokazuki. The translator gives it as the companion diver, and notes that a more literal rendering would be nearer to the one who dives alongside.
Maude reads the twelve accounts in one evening at her kitchen table and does not get up.

They are short. Most of them are less than a page. They were given by women in their fifties and sixties and seventies, to a man with a notebook, about things that had happened to them decades earlier, and there is no apparatus in them at all — no theory, no explanation, no religion to speak of. They read like people describing a thing that happens at work.
Most of the twelve are of themselves.

That is the first thing the translator flags in his preface and it is the thing Maude has to put the book down over. Not a stranger. Not a spirit with a shape of its own. The diver, herself, met at depth. Same size, same body, doing what she is doing.

Two of the twelve are of somebody else — one of a woman’s own mother, dead eleven years; one of a girl from the same village who had drowned the previous summer. One is of nothing visible at all, only a voice, and the voice was her own.
It does not attack. Not in any of the twelve. In eight of them it offers.

What it offers is shellfish. That is what it has in its hand, in eight separate accounts from eight women who did not know each other, taken down by a man with a notebook over a period of years — it holds out an abalone, prised loose, ready, and waits.
And every one of the twelve knows that you do not take it.

The tradition on that coast is completely unambiguous and it is unambiguous in the flat way that working practice is unambiguous, without any mysticism about it at all: if she offers you something you do not take it, and if she goes down you do not follow, and you surface, and you do not dive again that day.
The women who took it drowned.
There are two details that get up out of the book and stand in Maude’s kitchen with her.
The first is the mark.

In the accounts the companion is identical. That is stated and restated: identical, exact, the same in every particular, and this is what makes it what it is rather than a ghost or a woman from another village. And in six of the twelve there is one difference and it is the same difference.
The headband is too long.

The divers wore a cloth band round the head. The companion’s is longer. That is the whole of the mark — no wound, no wrongness of the face, no eyes that are not eyes. A working woman looks at a thing that is exactly herself in four metres of cold water and knows what she is looking at because of the length of a piece of cloth.
The second is the net.

Four of the twelve describe something between them. The translator struggles with the word and gives three options in a footnote, and the one he settles on is the light gauze that used to be hung over a bed against mosquitoes. A thin screen. Not a barrier — you can see through it and it does not hold you — and it is there, and its being there is the reason nothing has happened yet.
In two of the four accounts the woman describes the moment the screen was not there any more.
Both of those women describe it as the moment they went up.
The last thing in the collection is a page of the folklorist’s own notes and it is the reason Maude sits at the table until three in the morning.
He asked the women what the companion was. He asked all of them; he was a careful man and it was the obvious question.

None of them would give him an origin. He records this with visible frustration. Some said it was a diver who had drowned. Some said it was a warning, and that the warning came before a death and not after, so that it was a thing you were shown in advance. One said it was nothing at all and that she had been under too long and cold and that she still would not have taken the abalone.

And then he writes — and Maude reads this sentence four times — that the women of that coast did not appear to find the question interesting, and that what they cared about was not what it was but what you did, and that they had a great many charms sewn into their clothing and no theology whatsoever.

Two marks, stitched into the cloth. A five-pointed star drawn without lifting the needle, so that the line comes back to where it started, which the translator says was understood as: the diver returns. And a lattice, five one way and four the other, understood as a grid a thing cannot come through.
Maude turns the last page and there is nothing after it.
She rings her sister at ten past eight in the morning, which is the first time she has telephoned Sabine Vasseur rather than driven to her house in nine years.
“I’ve found something,” she says.
“Maude—”

“There are twelve of them. Written down in nineteen-thirty-nine off a coast on the other side of the world by a man with a notebook, from women who dived on one breath every day of their working lives for fifty years, and there is a word for it, and they all say the same thing, and one of them said it was shown to you in advance.”
There is a long silence on the line.
“Is it useful?” Sabine says.

And Maude, standing in her kitchen with a translated book from 1939 open on the counter and sixty-nine items in a file upstairs and a signed declaration of interest in a drawer she has not opened in five days, hears herself start to say yes, and stops, and stands there with her mouth open, and works it out.
Twelve accounts. Every one of them agrees. Do not take it, do not follow, surface, do not dive again that day.
There is nothing in the book about a man who has already taken it.

There is nothing in the book about what you do afterwards. Not one line, in twelve accounts and a folklorist’s notes and a translator’s preface, about a person who accepted and came up anyway. Because on that coast, in those accounts, that person does not come up. That is the entire content of the tradition. The women who took it drowned, and drowned women give no accounts, and so the thing Maude needs to know is precisely and exactly the thing that four hundred years of working practice on the other side of the world has no reason to have recorded.
She has the diagnosis. Complete, named, corroborated, four centuries deep and independently arrived at by thousands of women who never heard of a waste gas or of one another.
And it is Thursday, and he dives on Sunday, and there is not one word in any of it that tells her what to do.
“No,” she says. “It isn’t.”
TWENTY-ONE. 5 METRES
He brings her the notebook on the Saturday evening, which she has not asked for and which he has never once offered.
“I’ve finished it,” Aurel says.

They are in the hut. It is the last Saturday in July and the light is going and the heater is on because the heater is always on, and Sabine has the seventeen pages in a folder on the bench beside her because she has spent the afternoon at the Cut doing the thing she does instead of thinking, which is checking a line she has already checked.
“Finished what?”

“The sixth one.” He puts it on the bench. “I’m not going to write another. I’ve written every day for seventeen months and there’s nothing left to put in it, and I noticed on Wednesday that I was making things up to have something to write, and that seemed like a bad sign.”
“Aurel—”

“I’d like you to have it.” He is standing in the doorway with his hands in his coat pockets and he is entirely calm, and he has been entirely calm for three weeks, and it is the calm that has been frightening her since the fifteenth of July. “Not tonight. After tomorrow.”
“Why after?”
“Because if you read it tonight you won’t put ninety-four on the plate.”
Sabine looks at the notebook on the bench.
“And you want ninety-four.”
“I want it to be the last one,” he says. “That’s not the same thing and I know it isn’t. But it’s the truest way I can put it.”

He goes. She hears the car on the gravel and then the gate, and then the enormous silence that the Cut makes at the end of a day, which is not silence at all but the sound of four hundred thousand tonnes of water doing nothing.
She reads it in the hut with the heater on and her coat still buttoned.

She reads the floor. The three layers parting and then nothing left to part, thirty-two metres at one temperature with no edge in it anywhere. She reads about the grain stopping. She reads nothing is happening, nothing has ever happened, nothing is going to.
She reads the hand coming up and turning over and not waiting.
She reads I am not putting this in and I cannot find the moment and I know that I agreed to something. I know it the way you know you have signed for a parcel.

She reads the missed Thursday, and the forty-minute drive not taken, and the flatness where six years of Thursdays used to be, and the thumb across the back of the knuckles performed correctly for the first time in his life. She reads you would have to take out everybody and puts her hand over her mouth and sits like that for a while.
And then she turns the page, and there are eleven pages left, and they are dated across the last fortnight, and they are the last thing he wrote.

I have been going back over the whole of it, all of it, from the first notebook, because I have decided this is the final notebook and because I want the record to be complete, and in going back over it I have found something I got wrong from the very beginning.
I have been writing, since the fifth notebook, that there is somebody down there.
Singular. One. Arriving past thirty, on my left, a little below, falling at my rate.

That is not what has been happening and I do not know how I have failed to see it, and the only defence I can offer is that when you are told a thing arrives you look for the thing arriving and you do not count.
There are two.
There have always been two.

I have gone through every dive I can reconstruct and it holds all the way back to April. One on the left, a little below, which is the one I have written a hundred pages about. And one further out on the same side, beyond it, at the edge of where knowing anybody is there stops being knowing anything.

The second one has never come closer. Not once. Not at sixty, not at ninety-four, not at the floor when the first one turned to face me and the strap was too long and the scar was on the left hand where nobody but me could have put it. The near one closed the whole distance across a year and a half and the far one has held exactly where it has always held, at the outside edge, for a hundred and eleven dives.

It is not falling with us. That is the thing I want on the page. The near one falls at my rate and always has. The far one is simply there at every depth I pass, which is not the same, and I have thought about the difference for two weeks and the best I can do is this: the near one is coming down with me and the far one is already down.

It is smaller than me. Not by much. It has the attitude the near one has — head down, arms in — but it is not mine, and I have never once mistaken it for mine, and I have never told anybody about it because until this fortnight I did not know it was a fact. I have carried it the way you carry the weather.
It has never offered me anything.
Its hand is not out. In a hundred and eleven dives the hand has never come up.
It has something in it, and the hand is closed, and it is held in against the body the way you hold a thing you have been given and are not going to put down.
And the strap is too long.

I want to be careful because I have spent seventeen months being careful about a length of rubber. The near one’s strap is too long and I have written about it perhaps thirty times and it is the one wrong detail in a thing that is otherwise exactly me.
The far one’s is longer.

Not slightly. Very much longer, and wide rather than thin, and it goes back and up and it does not drift — that is the difference, that is the whole difference, it does not move at all. The near one’s strap drifts against the fall the way a strap would. The far one’s is straight and still and going up into the dark above us both like a line somebody is holding at the other end.

I do not know what to make of any of that and I am not going to invent something. I have put it in because I said at the start of the fourth notebook that I would put everything in, and because I am going to ask her for ninety-four on Sunday and after that I am going to give her the notebook.

She has known something since April. I have known that she has known since about May. I have never asked her, because in all this time of teaching myself out of books I have not once asked anybody anything, and because I understood early that if I asked she would tell me, and if she told me I would have to decide about it as a man on land with a kitchen and a mother and a Thursday, and I did not want to decide about it there.
I wanted to decide about it at the bottom.
I think that was the wrong way round and I think I have known that for a fortnight, and it is too late, and it was probably too late in April.
The last thing.
Whatever the far one is, it has been at the edge of every single dive I have done since I met the near one, and it has never come in, and it has never offered, and it has never gone.
It is not waiting for me.
It is not looking at me at all. I have never once had the sense of being attended to by it, and I have had the sense of being attended to by the near one from the first day.
It is facing up.
Sabine sits in the hut with the notebook open on her knees and the heater going and the light entirely gone outside.
She does not move for eleven minutes.

Then she gets up and goes out and down the ramp in the dark, and she does not put her hand in the water, and she gets in the car and drives home and takes the box out from under the stairs and takes the mask out of the box and sits on the floor of the hall with it in her lap.
It is nine years old and the skirt has gone hard and yellow.

And the strap is a wide black strap, the good kind, the kind you had to send away for then, and it is very long, because Elvire Baudry had a great deal of hair and wore it up under the strap in a knot the size of a fist, and she used to complain about the length of it, and she never once cut it down, and Sabine has run the whole of it through her fingers in the dark in this hallway perhaps four hundred times in nine years without ever letting herself finish the sentence.
It is facing up.

Not down at him. Not out at the dark. Up — at fifteen metres, at the surface, at a woman with her face in the water and a watch on her wrist and one arm through a buoy strap, holding station above a hole for nine years.

Sabine Vasseur sits on the floor of her hall at ten past one in the morning with her dead friend’s mask in her lap and understands that she has not been waiting to find out whether anybody else would say yes.
She has been being waited for.
The offer was never withdrawn. She wrote that in a document and signed it and sent it to her sister and she thought she was confessing.
She was reporting a fact and had the direction wrong. It is not that the hand is still out and she has been declining to go back.
It is that something has spent nine years standing at the edge of every dive that has ever been made in that water, holding what it was given, facing up, and it did not need her to come down.
It needed somebody to bring her to the edge and stand her there with a watch in her hand, forty times, at fifteen metres, with her face in the water, looking down.
She has done every bit of that herself. Nobody made her. She rigged the line, she set the plate, she wrote the times down in a good clear hand.
The phone is in the kitchen. It is ten past one and he is on nights and his phone is in a locker in a building on the Ossay road and he will not have it until six.

She rings it anyway, and it goes to nothing, and she says nothing into the nothing, and at twenty past one she puts her coat on over her nightclothes and drives out to the Cut and stands at the top of the ramp in the dark until it is light enough to see the buoy.
TWENTY-TWO. 0 METRES
The Sunday is the best day of the year, which is the sort of detail she will resent for the rest of her life.

No wind. The surface goes glass and holds the walls upside down in it. The water has come up four degrees since March and you can see the line for six metres instead of two, and there is not one thing wrong with the day, and nine people afterwards will say so independently.
The two medics come from the club forty miles off, because she rang them on the Wednesday and asked them to.
Maude comes at nine and takes up the position she has held for nine years — top of the ramp, eleven metres up, arms folded, glasses on. She has brought nothing with her. No bag, no laptop, no file.

Sabine rigs to a hundred and two and puts the plate at ninety-four, and she checks it three times, and she is aware while she is doing it that competence is a place to hide and that she has been hiding in it since April.
Aurel arrives at ten past ten and is entirely calm.
“You read it,” he says.
“I read it.”
“And you’ve rigged to a hundred and two.”
“I have.”
He nods slowly. He is looking out at the water and not at her. “There’s a version of this where you tell me what you know.”
“Yes.”
“Are you going to?”

And there it is. Not in a corridor when she was thirty-five. Not at her own kitchen table in June with the good lamp on. Here, at ten past ten on a Sunday morning in July, in daylight, sober, rested, with a folder on the bench and a notebook in her bag and nine years of it behind her, asked plainly by the one person entitled to ask.

Sabine Vasseur has, by her own account, twenty-two years of coaching, a hundred and eleven of his dives, four notebooks copied out in her own hand, seventeen pages signed and dated, and the whole of the fourth of April.
“There’s a woman on that coast in Japan,” she says, “who told a man with a notebook in nineteen-thirty-nine that it’s shown to you in advance. Not after. Before.”
“Shown to you as what?”
“As a warning.”
“Of what?”

And Sabine opens her mouth, and the day is beautiful, and the surface is glass, and the two medics are laying kit out on the platform and talking about somebody’s car, and her sister is at the top of the ramp forty metres away with her arms folded, and everything she needs to say is one sentence long and she has had nine years to compose it.
“Of nothing that can be helped,” she says.
Aurel considers this for a moment. Then he says, “That’s a third of it,” and it is the last thing he ever says to her that is not a number.
He goes to put his suit on.
He goes at 13:22.

The breathe-up is the best she has ever seen him do and she watches all of it, and at the roll she is at fifteen metres already with her face out and one arm through the buoy strap and a lanyard on, and he folds at the waist and comes past her, and her hand comes out and touches his shoulder as he goes by. She has done that every time since April and she does not think about it any more than she thinks about breathing.
Then the line goes taut.
There is one rope. There is the amount of tension in the rope. There is a watch.
She puts her face in the water and looks down.
Ninety-four metres. Down in one minute eight. Nothing at the plate. Ninety-four up.

She has told him five ten and she will begin to be unhappy at five forty and she will go at six, and she knows perfectly well that going at six achieves nothing at all, that she cannot reach thirty-one metres let alone ninety-four, that she has never in her life reached the place he is going, and that the entire safety apparatus she has constructed on this water since April amounts to a woman at fifteen metres with a watch, keeping station over a hole, looking down.
At two minutes the line has stopped moving.

At three she takes her face out and finds her sister at the top of the ramp, forty metres away and eleven metres up, and Maude is not looking at the water. Maude is looking at her. Has been, she understands, for the whole dive.
At four minutes she puts her face back in.
At five ten there is nothing.
At five forty there is nothing.
At six minutes Sabine Vasseur takes a breath and does not go.

She will never be able to say why, and she will be asked, and she will give four separate true reasons over the years and none of them will be it. She hangs at fifteen metres with her face in four-degree water and her heart down in the twenties and one arm through a buoy strap, looking down into a place where the colour has gone and then the not-colour has gone and then the grain has gone, and she does not go, and the honest account, which she will never give anybody, is that she was not permitted and she was not prevented.
She was expected.
At six twenty-eight the line moves.
He comes up out of the black at twenty metres and he comes up easily, on the same rhythm he went down on, and he comes past her, and as he passes her his hand comes out and touches her shoulder.

He has never done that. In a hundred and twelve dives it has always been her hand and his shoulder and never once the other way round, and she is still turning her head to follow the touch when he breaks the surface eight metres away.
Three breaths.
Small, then larger, then larger.

He reaches up and takes the mask off his face. Not pushed up onto the forehead. All the way off, and held, because the rule is that somebody has to see your eyes and there is no argument about whether they can see them through glass.
He finds her. He holds her eyes for a full three seconds, which is longer than it sounds when you are cold and your heart is somewhere down in the twenties and climbing.
He lifts his hand out of the water and makes a circle of his thumb and forefinger, and holds it up.
“I’m okay,” he says.
And it is perfect.
That is the whole of it and she will have it for the rest of her life. Every one of the four things, in order, correctly, at the right pace, in the right voice.

His eyes are steady. His pulse comes back up out of the twenties in the ordinary way under her fingers when she takes his wrist, because she takes his wrist, because that is the procedure and she follows procedure. He is shivering appropriately. He knows the date. He knows her name. He gives her his time, six minutes twenty-eight, and his depth, ninety-four metres, and both numbers are impossible and he gives them the way a man reads a bill.
There is no blood at the corner of his mouth.
She notices that and she will think about it for years.

On the platform one of the medics says something and the other one laughs. Up at the top of the ramp her sister has taken two steps forward and stopped, and is standing at the edge of the concrete with her arms at her sides, waiting.
Sabine looks at the young man treading water in front of her in a hole in the moor.

There is one thing she could do. It would take four seconds. She could say a name — hers, or the other one, or the word she now knows was written down in nineteen-thirty-nine by a man with a notebook — and watch his face, and know.

And if she is wrong she will have said it out loud, in daylight, on a Sunday, to a boy who works nights making clips, and it will be in the world, and she will have to live in a version of the world where she said it.
And if she is right—
She does not finish that. She has never once finished that, in nine years, and she is not going to start at fifteen minutes past two in the afternoon on the last Sunday in July.
“Time and depth,” she says. “Say them again.”
“Six twenty-eight. Ninety-four.”
“Good,” Sabine says.
She writes it down in a good clear hand.
Afterwards, when the kit is in the crates and the medics have gone and the notebook is in her bag and it is nearly six and the light has begun to go, Maude comes down the ramp.
All the way down. To the water.
The two of them stand at the bottom of the concrete for a while, side by side, not touching, looking out at the Cut, which is doing what it always does, which is nothing at all, patiently.
“You didn’t ask him,” Maude says.
“No.”

“You had it. You had all of it. You had nine years and seventeen pages and a book from nineteen-thirty-nine and a boy in front of you who’d have answered you, and you asked him for his time and his depth.”
“Yes.”
Maude nods.
“I didn’t submit the form,” she says.
“I know.”
“Nine years I’ve told myself I wanted to be told.” Maude takes her glasses off and holds them. “You told me. It’s the worst fortnight of my life. I’d give a great deal to have it back.”
“I know,” Sabine says.
They stand there.

“He’ll come back,” Maude says. It is not a question and it is not comfort. It is an item in a file. “Not this week. He’ll leave it a fortnight so it doesn’t look like a compulsion. Then he’ll ring you and ask what you’re putting on the plate.”
“Yes.”
“And you’ll be here.”

Sabine Vasseur looks at the black water in the hole that six generations of Ossay dug dry and one generation let fill, and she thinks about a wide strap, very long, straight and still, going up into the dark above everybody, like a line somebody is holding at the other end.
“Yes,” she says.
Then she crouches at the edge of the water, the way she does at the end of every day, and puts her right hand in past the wrist.

The cold comes up through her wrist like a note being struck. The switch throws, because the switch is not hers and never has been, and her heart goes long in her throat, and she counts, and at nineteen she does not take her hand out.
She stays there, crouched at the edge, with her hand in it, in the last of the light, for a long time.
